https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.subtitle: If elected London mayor, I will trigger a housing revolution that gives young people the chance to embrace conservative values
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.text:
We are told that London is a “Labour city”. This is a myth, and it would be a mistake for us to believe it. While it is true that Conservative politics is not as popular in the capital as we would like it to be at this moment, conservative ideas are as popular as ever – and always will be.
Millions of people live by conservative values every single day: working hard to provide for their family, believing in law and order, respecting our history, wanting to put down roots and be part of a community, and loving the place we call home. They might not walk around with a blue rosette, but their values are our values. Indeed, conservatism can thrive in London. My plan is to achieve that next year, not in generations’ time.
I am standing to be the Conservative candidate for the next London mayoral election. And I want us to solve the one issue that will cause serious damage if we fail to tackle it now: housing. Conservatism cannot succeed without good housing that people can afford to buy. If you spend years working hard but can barely rent a studio flat, then it will feel like conservatism does not have much to offer you – and you wouldn’t be wrong.
As things stand, it is far too difficult for younger people to lay down roots, put money aside for their future and think about having children of their own. It is difficult to feel a sense of home if you’re forced to move from houseshare to houseshare, not even having time to get to know your neighbours. Here and elsewhere, we see how those who may be open to conservative values find little opportunity to live by them.
Rather than bonding with their neighbourhood, some young people are instead finding community in the dreadful, online, American-style identity politics that is causing so much division these days. Sadiq Khan, who’s now been London’s mayor for the best part of a decade, has capitalised on this anger and division. He taps into the worst of identity politics and shakes hands with Extinction Rebellion activists who seem intent on causing disruption and chaos.
He does not offer any solutions himself. He is a protest politician, better known for his Twitter fights with Trump than doing anything for London. No surprise, then, that he is also failing spectacularly at building homes, throwing together tower blocks of one-bedroom flats where people can’t lay down roots, and barely keeping up with his targets despite receiving billions in government money.
Sadiq Khan has filled the vacuum that conservatism has left behind by failing to give people the homes they need. And so long as that vacuum remains, he does not need to deliver anything but platitudes and empty promises. So it is imperative that we solve this crisis. If I am the mayoral candidate, I will win in London with a serious plan to build homes.
We will do it in the right way, and in the right places. They will be homes that people want to live in, which do not disrupt existing communities.
The best model for this is Create Streets, a brilliant project set up by Nicholas Boys Smith to promote the creation of beautiful, green, community-oriented places which are high density but not high rise. As mayor, I would roll out this model at scale across London, working with local boroughs and developers as part of an ambitious, common sense London Plan.
I would deliver this while minimising the impact on existing communities, ensuring new-builds have the necessary infrastructure in place, and all without building on the Green Belt. A lot more homes, in the right places. That is what I will deliver, if made the Conservative candidate.
Susan Hall is a member of the London Assembly

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.subtitle: Keir Starmer continues to take money from Dale Vince, founder of Ecotricity, despite UK entering the fifth week of disruption
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.text:
Suella Braverman has accused Sir Keir Starmer of being “in bed” with Just Stop Oil’s donors as he faced calls to hand back £1.5 million Labour has received from one of the environmental group’s major backers.
The Home Secretary said the Labour leader was “happy to take bundles of cash” in private from Dale Vince, who helped bankroll the setting up of the green protest movement, whilst publicly condemning its actions.
She and other senior Tories said there were questions to answer over whether Sir Keir was going “soft on crime” as a result or receiving the money.
Their intervention came ahead of more planned action by Just Stop Oil that ministers have warned will heap “misery” on ordinary families and workers in London.
Mrs Braverman told the Telegraph: “While this government cracks down on Just Stop Oil eco-zealots, Keir Starmer and the Labour Party have taken £1.5million in donations from the ‘green businessman’ who bankrolls these selfish protesters.
“It’s the same old Labour Party, soft on crime and soft on criminals. Sir Keir Starmer claims to be on the side of hard-working Brits whose lives are disrupted by these idiots but behind the scenes he’s happy to take bundles of cash from one of their biggest donors.
“He had the cheek to claim Labour is no longer the party of protest this year - the reality is he’s in bed with their donors.
“Perhaps that explains why Sir Keir and his Labour Party repeatedly voted against our measures to give police the powers they requested so these eco-zealots can be taken off our streets and put behind bars.”
Mr Vince, the founder of green energy firm Ecotricity, has given around £1.5 million to Labour over the past decade. He is said to be worth £100 million.
Greg Hands urged Sir Keir Starmer to hand back the cash.
His donations have included £20,000 to Sir Keir’s office and £10,000 to his deputy Angela Rayner, according to Electoral Commission data.
There is no suggestion Mr Vince sought to influence Labour policy with the donations.
Just Stop Oil sparked fury on Thursday when three of its activists threw paint all over a garden at the Chelsea Flower Show. Three people were arrested on suspicion of criminal damage in relation to the incident, the Metropolitan Police later said in a statement.
The climate group has been conducting a fifth “week of action” in London which has also seen activists walking slowly in the road to stop traffic.
In a letter to Anneliese Dodds, the Labour chairman, Mr Hands said it was time for her party to hand back the money donated by Mr Vince.
He wrote: “In previous years this planned action on our capital has resulted in ambulance delays and traffic chaos causing misery amongst Londoners.
“Since 2014, the Labour Party has taken £1.5 million in donations from one of Extinction Rebellion and Just Stop Oil’s biggest donors, Dale Vince.
“Keir Starmer and Angela Rayner have together taken £30,000. Mr Vince congratulated Just Stop Oil on their attack at the World Snooker Championship, calling the attack ‘good work’.
“Given these attacks, I am calling on you to return these donations. I am concerned about the influence of this money given the Labour Party’s decision to vote against tougher measures to stop disruption via the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act.
“I note the Labour Party has already caved into the demands made by the group and announced a halt to new oil, gas and coal projects.
“I am not writing to discuss the merits of that decision and this letter is not the place to debate the damage that policy will have to UK tax revenues or job losses. I can assure you the Conservative Government will not negotiate with these activists.”
Just Stop Oil has previously targeted major cultural and sporting events including Premier League football matches and this year’s World Snooker Championships.
On Saturday, activists from the group launched a pitch invasion midway through the Rugby Premiership final between Saracens and Sale at Twickenham .
Samuel Johnson, 40, of Reydon, Suffolk, and Patrick Hart, 37, of Brislington, Bristol, were charged with aggravated trespass, the Met said.
In a statement released after the match the force was scathing of the group’s activities across London in recent weeks and months.
Commander Kyle Gordon said: "To date we have seen 102 slow marches across London by Just Stop Oil that has caused serious disruption and frustration to those going about their business in the city leading to 51 arrests to date.
"Similarly, yesterday's incident at the rugby final will have caused frustration to both the players and spectators alike.
"With many other events taking place, and visitors in our capital this weekend, we will continue to monitor and respond to such incidents quickly.
"Where protest moves into criminality or serious disruption, we will take robust action to ensure Londoners and visitors alike can continue to enjoy their bank holiday weekend."
On Sunday, it emerged that Sir Keir is set to announce a Labour government would end all new oil and gas exploration in the North Sea.
The Labour Party was contacted for comment.
Sir Keir has previously denied any suggestion that his decision making would be affected by such donations.
In April he said: "He knows that nothing he donates to the Labour Party is going to affect my judgment on this. The fact he donates will not make a blind bit of difference to the tough line I take in relation to Just Stop Oil."

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/royal-family.text:
Thank you for joining us on a momentous day in British history.
The Coronation of King Charles and Queen Camilla will live long in the memory of the thousands inside Westminster Abbey, the massive crowds on the streets of London, and the millions watching around the world.
Join us tomorrow morning for coverage of the Big Lunch and later the Coronation Concert.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky has congratulated the King on his Coronation.
In his nightly address to the Ukrainian people, Mr Zelensky on Saturday night wished the King “many years of successful reign”.
Ukraine’s president did not attend the ceremony at Westminster Abbey but his country was represented by Olena Zelenska, the First Lady, and Denys Shmyhal, the Prime Minister.
The King sent a letter to his former crew mates on the morning of his Coronation to thank them for their professionalism, good humour and the “strong bonds” they forged, it has emerged.
His Majesty wrote to all the individuals who served under him when he was in command of the minesweeper HMS Bronington almost 50 years ago.
The King was in charge of the vessel between Feb 9 1976 and Dec 15 1976. The boat was decommissioned in 1988 and was one of the last wood-walled naval vessels, with a hull made of mahogany.
Read more: King thanks former HMS Bronington shipmates on morning of Coronation
Lord Andrew Lloyd Webber's coronation anthem will be heard in Sunday services across the country this weekend as the sheet music has been sent to thousands of churches.
The theatre impresario's song, Make A Joyful Noise, was performed publicly for the first time as the King was enthroned on Saturday.
Following the ceremony, the music was distributed to 6,000 churches to allow them the chance to perform it during their own services on Sunday and over the coming weeks.
During the coronation, the opening and closing fanfare of the piece was played by the fanfare trumpeters of the Royal Air Force - while the chorus was sung by The Choir of Westminster Abbey.
Watch the video for the Coronation Anthem below:
The Telegraph's overnight team will be guiding you through the rest of the night on this live blog.
On a truly remarkable day, no amount of rain could dampen the spirits of well-wishers lining the streets of London or the significance of the first occasion of its kind in 70 years as King Charles and Queen Camilla were crowned.
In the biggest ceremonial display of pomp and circumstance in seven decades, the King vowed: "I come not to be served but to serve."
From a sword-wielding leader of the Commons to a musical score that blended a new Coronation Anthem with the soulful tones of a gospel choir and classics including Zadok the Priest, Saturday surmised so much of what is great about Britain.
The celebrations do not end with nightfall on Saturday, as revellers take part in the Big Lunch across the country before the Coronation Concert comes to Windsor Castle, and The Telegraph will once again be keeping you up to date all throughout tomorrow. Vivat Rex.
Celebrations for the coronation of King Charles, which kicked off today, have spurred some of the biggest community get-togethers in British history.
At the heart of festivities will be street parties across the country through the Coronation Big Lunch, with members of the public urged to attend or even host events. More than 7,000 are already thought to have been registered.
Into tomorrow evening, Katy Perry and Take That top the bill at the Coronation Concert at Windsor Castle. A-listers Tom Cruise and Dame Joan Collins are also billed to contribute to the evening's entertainment.
Even Winnie-the-Pooh will be making a special appearance, while the new Time Lord Ncuti Gatwa is taking a break from filming the upcoming series of Doctor Who to participate.
Just two days earlier, she was cradling a pint in the Dog and Duck and taking a trip on the Tube.
She may not have been the one being crowned at Westminster Abbey on Saturday, but as she dazzled the crowds in a stunning ivory Alexander McQueen gown, the Princess of Wales once again proved herself to be the queen of royal style.
Her intricate silk crepe dress featuring silver bullion and thread work embroidery in the shape of patriotic roses, thistles, daffodils and shamrocks naturally invited comparisons to her wedding day in 2011 - when she wore the same designer at the same venue.
But it was the Jess Collett x Alexander McQueen headpiece that really set the mother-of-three apart from the rest of the congregation.
Made with silver bullion, crystal and silver threadwork in three-dimensional embroidery, the beautiful piece was part headpiece, part floral garland.
How the Princess of Wales showed us the monarchy's future is assured
Don't reign on my parade. At least, please don't rain on my reign, or so Charles III must have thought this morning. In the past, our former Prince of Wales was known to be prone to gloom, writes Allison Pearson.
The dear chap had waited 70 years for his Coronation. You prayed that the awfully British weather had not dampened his spirits. The sky over Buckingham Palace changed from pale pigeon to a menacing pewter. Would it cast a pall over the big day or could our longest-serving Prince of Wales come up smiling as the sun king? In short, would Eeyore be transformed by his people's affection into Winnie the Pooh.Not long after 8am, BBC1 commentator Clare Balding was determinedly upbeat. "Only a 40 per cent chance of showers," she boomed in that ebullient, jolly-hockey-sticks style that suits these great national occasions so well.Translated from broadcasterese, 40 per cent chance of showers meant: "It'll bucket down." Clare skilfully stopped us dwelling on that possibility by somehow knowing the name of every horse that would be on parade.A friend who had camped overnight on the Mall texted me: "Mood wonderful. Portable lavatories locked." Quintessentially British, then. We can do squeezed sphincters, as well as stiff upper lips, should the need arise.
Allison Pearson: What a remarkable mix of pageantry, religion, history, military display and nostalgia
If they needed any reassurance that the country was right behind them, the King and Queen received it in spectacular style as they appeared on the Buckingham Palace balcony for the first time since the Accession, writes Gordon Rayner, The Telegraph's Associate Editor.
Hundreds of thousands of well-wishers in The Mall, unperturbed by the dismal weather, roared their appreciation for the couple as they emerged wearing their crowns and Coronation robes.
The King has been making appearances on the Buckingham Palace balcony since he was two years old, but still seemed taken aback by the reception he received, telling the Queen: "Oh my goodness, it’s wonderful this is."
Crowds chanting "God Save the King" were even treated to an encore as the royal couple re-emerged on the balcony for a second appearance, to the delight of those who had patiently waited - for days in some cases - to be part of the event.
Not even the King’s 1981 balcony moment after his wedding to Diana, Princess of Wales held such significance for him as this one, and few in recent memory have been as significant for the monarchy.
Read more: How the love of the crowds took the King by surprise
First came the pomp and pageantry, then the ancient, most solemn ritual under the eyes of God.
As cries of "Vivat Rex Carolus" and "Vivat Regina Camilla" rang out in Westminster Abbey, the King and Queen took their place in the history books just as he had always hoped: together.
As man and wife, King and Queen, this was the moment they and millions watching around the world could finally embrace a new Carolean era.
For King Charles III, it was the most important and sacred ceremony of his long public life. As Queen Camilla was crowned, he permitted himself a small smile of irrepressible emotion: the culmination of a long, and at one point unlikely, journey to their thrones.
Hannah Furness, our Royal Editor, has this must-read front page story
For Tim Stanley, the Coronation was a moving testament of history and faith:
This was the moment Charles was transformed, bodily, into a King – and yet he’s never seemed more human or so close. Literally in my case because I blagged a seat in the north transept of the Abbey. To attend a service like this is to witness ancient magic, albeit 200 yards away, on tiptoes and through the narrow gap between fascinator hats.Guests had to arrive by 7am. My breakfast was a shared bag of jelly babies. The Dean walked quickly down the nave; in his hands was the silver urn containing the holy chrism oil, held aloft and with great care, as if it were gelignite.
Meanwhile, the joke among royal reporters is that we always get seated behind a pillar – "mum will get a better view off the telly" – but someone had kindly hung up a TV set for us to watch. Alas, due to technical difficulties, the screen was frozen – on an image of a church pillar.Never mind! There was plenty more to look at. Morning suits and medals, island potentates and one aristocrat (he had to be an aristocrat) wandering about, shirt untucked, hopelessly lost. Katy Perry, Lionel Ritchie, Andrew Lloyd Webber; the Abbey was Madame Tussauds come to life, with Jill Biden representing the rebel republic, satisfyingly given a seat on the back row. One hopes far behind a lucky lollipop lady and the Duke of Milton Keynes.
Read Tim Stanley's first draft of history in full
"Not everyone is excited about the Coronation," said Naga Munchetty at the moment I tuned into the BBC’s coverage at breakfast time. That's our Naga, ever the ray of sunshine. To be fair, though, it wasn’t just our national broadcaster who found today a slightly awkward occasion.
Yes, coverage across the board was largely respectful and professional, with the standard preamble – visiting the horses at Hyde Park Barracks, vox pops with people wearing those Union Jack umbrella-hats – followed by a focus on the pageantry and spectacle of the procession and the ceremony. But at times there was something apologetic about it.
David Olusoga, on the BBC, pointed out that the terminology of the oath will be "very uncomfortable" for some to hear because they will feel it doesn’t represent their beliefs.
ITV invited on a royal historian, Anna Whitelock, who explained that today’s proceedings could ignite a sense of injustice "because it's about inequality, about a sense of obedience and allegiance to one man… one man who’s there not for anything he's done, but simply that he was born into a white privileged family".
Anita Singh: Which broadcasters did a decent job - and who struggled?
The Prince and Princess of Wales have released a video capturing the events of today, from their family setting off to the Coronation to the unforgettable scene on the balcony this afternoon.
You can watch it below:
Musically, this was the coronation that was going to break the mould, writes Ivan Hewitt. The King wanted a more diverse and inclusive ceremony, and the music had to reflect that. Girl choristers would be involved for the first time ever, as well as a gospel choir, a Greek orthodox choir, and two distinguished black soloists.
And there were to be no fewer than 12 brand-new pieces. But when the full list of music was disclosed, it seemed like business as usual. William Byrd, Edward Elgar, Walford Davies, Vaughan Williams, Handel, Parry – all the names familiar from every coronation since 1902 were there.
So in setting the musical tone of this first coronation of the 21st century, who would win out? Would it be Sir Hubert Parry, or Lord Lloyd-Webber, composer of the brand-new Coronation anthem Make a Joyful Noise? The answer you may not be surprised to hear was Sir Hubert Parry, whose great anthem, I was Glad, performed by the Abbey and Chapel Royal Choirs plus those girl choristers together with the orchestra rang out at the very moment when the King and Queen entered the Abbey.
It was stupendously performed at a firm pace – it’s all too easy for things to drag in the cavernous acoustic of the Abbey – and the fanfares and acclamations from the boy and girl choristers were startlingly vivid. After the moment of reflectiveness in the middle, the thrilling "turn" of the harmony as the music drives towards its magnificent ending would have melted the heart of the sternest republican.
Ivan Hewitt: Barely a ripple of discomfort as old meets new
The King and Queen’s balcony appearance after their historic crowning reflected the new slimmed down monarchy.
Their Majesties, leading the rest of the working family out for the first time as King, were flanked by 15 other members of the Royal family - but some familiar faces were missing.
Among the most notable who missed out on the Buckingham Palace appearance were the Duke of York and the Duke of Sussex, who did not take any formal role at the Coronation due to not being working Royals anymore.
Princesses Beatrice and Eugenie, the Duke of York’s two daughters, were also not present for the traditional moment.
Instead of joining the rest of his family at the palace after the service, the King's second son chose to fly back home to California immediately to kiss his son Archie goodnight on his fourth birthday.
India McTaggart, our Royal Correspondent, has all the details
Leader of the House of Commons Penny Mordaunt has emerged as the quiet star of the Coronation ceremony – one that nobody saw coming.
Carrying out her role as Lord President of the Privy Council, Mordaunt’s stylish appearance soon sparked comparisons to Pippa Middleton’s show-stealing performance at the Prince and Princess of Wales’s wedding in 2011.
For the ceremony, Mordaunt was required to carry the 17th-Century Sword of State into the Abbey in the King's Procession, and continue to hold it aloft for much of the service – specifically at right angles to her body. The sword, decorated with royal symbols including the lion and union and fleur de lis, is also used during the state opening of Parliament.
Given its 4ft (121cm) length and 8lb (3.5kg) weight, this is no mean feat, as evidenced by her shaking arms, when she handed the historic weapon to King Charles.
She had prepared for the moment though, drawing on her training as a Royal Navy reservist to ensure that she could hold it aloft for the whole ceremony. “[I] will be carrying the Sword of State, which is the heaviest sword, so I’ve been doing some press-ups to train for that," she told The Times Red Box podcast prior to the event. The Sword represents the King's authority, she explained. "It was one of two swords made for Charles II and only one survives.
Tamara Abraham has the story
It took me a second to work out what Prince Harry reminded me of as he made his way down the aisle of Westminster Abbey today, writes Celia Walden.
Then it came to me: the royal renegade had the expression and gait of a teenager who had recently disgraced himself at a family occasion, necking a bottle of port and telling auntie Mabel she looked like a horse before throwing up on the sitting room carpet.
Like that teen, Harry had only agreed to come to the next big family do under duress. But he certainly wasn't going to apologise for his actions, hence the slightly bowed head, the set jaw and the defiance in his demeanour.
Had the 38-year-old expat been able to chew gum, he would have been masticating furiously all the way to his seat… in the third row, where he couldn't have looked like more of a "spare" had a woman in a large, feathered hat not immediately seated herself in front, obliterating him from public view. Which Princess Anne promptly did.
Celia Walden: Harry was always goign to make the briefest of visits
There are two Windsor males to celebrate this week – one will be on the receiving end of a tad more pomp and ceremony than the other, but both will be basking in the limelight of a meticulously planned party.
Yes, it’s Prince Archie's fourth birthday, and the eldest child of Montecito’s best-connected couple is likely to have an event with a curated guest list and thoughtfully planned food and entertainment. Just like his grandfather, King Charles.
After all, this birthday is the reason his mother isn't coming to the Coronation, and why Harry is flying home three hours after the ceremony ends (the time difference means he could catch the tail end of a late-afternoon celebration).
Prince Archie Harrison Mountbatten-Windsor may be seventh in line to the British throne and the grandchild of the reigning monarch, but he apparently speaks with a thick American accent. According to sources close to the couple, he is "thriving" in his new Californian life, he loves running on the beach and playing in his park-sized "backyard".
Melissa Twigg has more here
The Metropolitan Police has said it can "absolutely understand public concern" after the arrests it made this morning.
In a statement, the force said 52 arrests had been made throughout the day for offences including affray, public order offences, breach of the peace and conspiracy to cause a public nuisance.
Commander Karen Findlay hailed the "magnificent team effort" of her colleagues, adding: "We absolutely understand public concern following the arrests we made this morning.
"Protest is lawful and it can be disruptive. We have policed numerous protests without intervention in the build-up to the Coronation, and during it. Our duty is to do so in a proportionate manner in line with relevant legislation. We also have a duty to intervene when protest becomes criminal and may cause serious disruption.“This depends on the context. The Coronation is a once in a generation event and that is a key consideration in our assessment."
The Princess Royal was praised as the "best rider on parade" as she rode behind the newly crowned King and Queen in the Coronation procession.
The former Olympic rider followed the King and Queen, who were in the Gold State Coach, on horseback during the large military procession back to Buckingham Palace.
Clare Balding, who was commentating on this part of the Coronation for the BBC, said: "I think fair to say she's the best rider on parade; she's a former Olympian, a European Open champion as well, so she knows what she's doing.
"She's riding a horse called Faulkand, looking extremely comfortable en route."
India McTaggart, our Royal Correspondent, has the story
The point at which the public was asked to swear allegiance to their monarch during the Coronation was always going to be controversial.
Days of debate had raged over whether it was too anachronistic and out of touch in a modern democracy - and over how the crowds would react.
Shortly after the King was crowned, the Archbishop of Canterbury invited everyone, not just the congregation in Westminster Abbey, to offer their support, either through a "moment of private reflection", or by reciting the oath in full.
In the end, the crowds lining the Mall, in Green Park and in Hyde Park appeared overwhelmingly to opt for the former.
Judith Woods has more here
Liverpool fans have booed God Save the King in the past few minutes when it was played before kick-off at Anfield.
Supporters jeered the National Anthem prior to their fixture against Brentford:
Scottish nationalists have used coronation day as an opportunity to promote independence with former first minister Alex Salmond leading a rally in Glasgow, writes Neil Johnston.
Mr Salmond told the All Under One Banner march which organisers claimed was attended by more than 20,000 people to shout louder for "the benefit of those in Westminster Abbey".
The Alba Party leader told the crowd at the rally which coincided with the coronation ceremony: "In London, the subjects are required to swear an oath of allegiance to the Crown.
"In Scotland, in Glasgow, the citizens choose to swear an oath of loyalty to Scotland. The homage of the people is now to be said silently - which will stop people having to swear at their TV sets."
Claiming the march was "one of the greatest in Scotland ever", Mr Salmond called for parties backing Scottish independence to stand together at the election in seeking a mandate. He then led the crowd in a chant calling for independence, urging them to shout louder "for the benefit of those in Westminster Abbey".
A Telegraph reader who left his son's wedding in Greece to attend the Coronation said it was "absolutely worth it".
Geoff Norris, 55, was delighted when he discovered that he was one of the lucky 2,200 people selected to attend - but was crestfallen when his wife pointed out the date clashed with his son's nuptials.
Mr Norris recevied a coveted invitation after being awarded a British Empire Medal for services to the local community during the pandemic following his efforts to deliver food to the vulnerable.
Describing his reaction to being invited, Mr Norris said: "I was chuffed as hell, obviously! I was very proud and honoured."
Full story: 'It was so intense but very, very personal'
Boris Johnson secured a better seat in the Coronation congregation than serving Cabinet ministers, with a front row view on a pew next to other former prime ministers.
The Conservative MP could be seen with his wife, Carrie, in the choir seats of Westminster Abbey, next to Theresa May and her husband Philip.
Almost all Cabinet ministers who attended were relegated to the back row on the far end of the choir, behind Lord Lloyd-Webber.
Jeremy Hunt, Ben Wallace, Michael Gove and other ministers lined up on a pew to watch their colleague, Penny Mordaunt, carry the Sword of State in the King's procession into the Abbey.
BBC viewers switched over channels to watch the King’s Coronation after a series of technical glitches disrupted its coverage.
As early as 7.30am, viewers were left staring at a multicoloured screen for nearly a whole minute during a live broadcast before technicians fixed the error.
Instead of troops marching along the Mall in full regalia towards Westminster Abbey, its audience was shown coloured bars which said "BBC North Salford MediaCityUK Tech Ops North".
Other technical hiccups occurred throughout the day with viewers complaining of audio broadcasts breaking up and hearing interference from production staff.
Read the full story here
Jill Biden has spoken about meeting the King and the Princess of Wales at a Buckingham Palace reception held on the eve of the Coronation.
Dr Biden, the First Lady of the United States who led a delegation in place of her husband Joe, said the King had asked her to "give my best to your husband".
She added of her conversation with Princess Kate: "[Kate] said she didn't know if her son could sit still for two hours and we just had a good laugh over it. It's just something, I think, that's common to a lot of us."
Dr Biden described the Coronation itself, where she sat next to Olena Zelenska, Ukraine's First Lady, as "just amazing to see".
She told the Associated Press: "You can’t imagine that moment where you actually see the crown being placed on the head of the King and then on the head of the Queen. I felt as I sat there, I felt this sense of decorum and civility that binds together people of all nations."
Republican France is captivated by the Coronation of King Charles III, writes James Allen in Paris, as all major TV news channels and newspapers wiped out their usual schedules to cover the Coronation live .
TF1 – France’s national broadcaster – sent its star presenters to London as Philip Corbé, editorial director of BFM, the 24-hour news channel, said his team in London was supported by "experts in Royalty and experts in international politics".
And papers including Le Parisien – the leading tabloid in the French capital – put the story on their front page, and also produced special supplements.
'Let the Party Begin!' was the front page headline on Le Parisien, while Ouest France (West France) – the biggest provincial paper in the country – led with: 'The United Kingdom is ready for the coronation of its King Charles III'.
There were garden and street parties planned across France, with the most prestigious at the British Embassy in Paris.
The King was worried about the timing of his own Coronation after arriving at Westminster Abbey six minutes early and before his son.
King Charles and Queen Camilla remained in their horse-drawn carriage for six minutes outside the Abbey's Great West Door prior to the Coronation.As the King and Queen waited patiently, two Bentleys and a security vehicle pulled up behind, carrying the Prince and Princess of Wales and their two youngest children.Eventually the King and Queen entered the Abbey with the Prince and Princess walking behind them. It appears the problems were caused by King Charles arriving early.
Robert Mendick and Christopher Hope have this report
The Right Reverend Paul Butler, Bishop of Durham, told Sky News how he had found being one of the two bishops assistant to the King, writes Catherine Lough.
"That meant I was at the King's right hand from greeting him when he arrived at the west gate to saying farewell to him at the west door at the end of the ceremony.

For nearly 1,000 years, monarchs have been crowned in Westminster Abbey. Now, Charles III has followed in the footsteps of the 39 Kings and Queens who came before him, including his mother Elizabeth II and his grandfather George VI, in his own Coronation.
Many monarchs have sought to put their own spin on the Coronation, including two major revisions and a translation from Latin to English, but the core ceremony can be traced back to as early as the crowning of King Edgar in 973 AD.
Our vivid historic record allows us to see just how well preserved this element of our history is. Beyond the paintings and historic transcripts, however, archive footage from the 20th-century coronation ceremonies reveals how just little this ancient ceremony has changed.

The British national anthem may be much-loved on its home turf – apart from among die-hard republicans – but it has to be said it’s not exactly exciting.
It doesn’t have the jollity of the Italian or quite a few Latin American national anthems, which sound like operatic choruses with new words attached.
It lacks the excitement of the Marseillaise, with its cry of “To Arms, Citizens!” or the lovely poetry of the Bangladeshi anthem, which rhapsodises “In Spring, O mother, the fragrance from your mango groves makes me wild with joy.”
The lyrics are a sober prayer, uttered in stately triple time, with just a touch of excitement at the crescendo which leads from the third line up to the fourth beginning “Send him victorious.”

The King has removed the St Edward’s Crown, and is now wearing the Imperial State Crown. It is known as a working crown as it is used on many state occasions, notably the annual State Opening of Parliament.
Made in 1937, it is a relatively new addition to the collection, its design based on Queen Victoria's earlier Imperial State Crown. The orb and the cross on the top were transferred directly over from the original.
It is made of gold and set with 2,868 diamonds, the largest of which is the Cullinan II.
The King and Queen proceed out of the Abbey. The King is wearing the Imperial Robe, also referred to as the Robe of Estate, and carrying the Sceptre and Orb.
The robe, which is the same one worn by Queen Elizabeth in 1953, is embroidered with 18 types of gold thread and took 12 embroiders more than 3,500 hours to complete between March and May 1953.
A fanfare sounds, and all stand to sing the National Anthem
God save our gracious King, long live our noble King, God save The King! Send him victorious, happy and glorious, long to reign over us, God save The King!
Thy choicest gifts in store on him be pleased to pour, long may he reign: May he defend our laws, and ever give us cause to sing with heart and voice God save The King!
God Save The King has been the national anthem for more than 250 years. But the phrase itself is much older, appearing multiple times in The King James Bible.
There was a touching moment between the King and Prince of Wales as the latter paid homage, the only blood prince to do so, in a break with tradition.
The Prince appeared to avoid eye contact with his father through much of the homage.
He then kissed the King on the cheek and his father was seen to say a few words to his elder son.
The choir is singing the hymn Te Deum Laudamus, which is sometimes referred to as The Hymn of the Church.
It dates to the fourth century and has always been part of the Coronation Rite.
This setting of the Hymn was written by Sir William Walton (1902-83) for Queen Elizabeth’s Coronation in 1953.
During the Hymn the King and Queen move into St Edward’s Chapel behind the High Altar, where they change into the Robes of Estate, and the King changes the St Edward’s Crown for the Imperial State Crown.
The Archbishop is delivering the post-Communion prayer, which is a Collect from the Service of Holy Communion in the Book of Common Prayer.
It asks God to direct all of us in his holy ways, so that we may live lives of service, and know his divine protection and peace.
O ALMIGHTY Lord, and everlasting God, vouchsafe, we beseech thee, to direct, sanctify, and govern both our hearts and bodies, in the ways of thy laws, and in the works of thy commandments; that through thy most mighty protection, both here and ever, we may be preserved in body and soul; through our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. Amen.
The choir sings Agnus Dei, during which Their Majesties receive Holy communion.
Agnus Dei is Latin for ‘Lamb of God’. This was the title used by St John the Baptist to describe Jesus. It probably became part of the Communion service in the seventh century as a chant to be sung as the bread and wine were prepared for distribution.
O LAMB of God, that takest away the sins of the world, have mercy upon us. O Lamb of God, that takest away the sins of the world, have mercy upon us. O Lamb of God, that takest away the sins of the world, grant us thy peace.

All eyes were on the Duke on Saturday as he sat with his relatives in public for the first time since he criticised them in his memoir, Spare.
Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; thy will be done; on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us. And lead us not into temptation; but deliver us from evil. For thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory, for ever and ever. Amen.
The version of the prayer is based on Jesus’s words as they are recorded in Matthew’s Gospel.
The Coronation has always been set within the context of the Eucharist, or Holy Communion, which is the principal act of worship in the Christian church.
The central part of the prayer recalls the words of Jesus over the bread and wine at the Last Supper.
The beginning of the prayer takes words used at the late Queen’s Coronation in 1953 and adds further words from the Bible which continue to reinforce the theme of loving service.
The choir then sings the Sanctus, which has been a consistent part of the Eucharistic Prayer since the fifth century. It was composed for the Coronation by Rozanna Panufnik.
We've just watched the King and Queen be crowned and sit on their thrones.
Here's a guide to the layout and what it all symbolises.
The Archbishop of Canterbury delivers the prayer over the bread and wine.
It is a translation of another praye found in the Liber Regalia (king’s book), which is one of the oldest sources for the Coronation service.
Bless, O Lord, we beseech thee, these thy gifts, and sanctify them unto this holy use, that by them we may be made partakers of the Body and Blood of thine only-begotten Son Jesus Christ, and fed unto everlasting life of soul and body: And that thy servant King Charles may be enabled to the discharge of his weighty office, whereunto of thy great goodness thou hast called and appointed him. Grant this, O Lord, for Jesus Christ’s sake, our only Mediator and Advocate. Amen.
The Hymn, Christ is made the sure foundation, is being sung by the congregation to the Westminster Abbey tune, which comes from the end of HEnry Purcell’s anthem O God thou art my God.
The words of the hymn are over one thousand years old and are based on passages from the Old and New Testaments and Psalms.
During the hymn, breads and wine are brought before the King for him to acknowledge and make formal presentation of them as they are taken to the High Altar.
The anthem for the Enthroning, titled The Queen is Make a Joyful Noise, is by the composer Andrew Lloyd Webber.
The words are from Psalm 98 Make a joyful noise unto the Lord for he hath done marvellous things and his holy arm hath gotten him the victory.' It's the grandest of the new pieces.
Finally, Queen Camilla joins His Majesty on her throne beside his. The visual is meant to show the royal couple united in their joint vocation before God. The anthem being sung was composed by Lord Andrew Lloyd-Webber.
The Bishop of Dover presents the rod and Lord Chartres presents the sceptre. In accepting these the Consort acknowledges the responsibilities and duties which come with undertaking to support her husband and her sovereign.
“Receive the Royal Sceptre and the Rod of equity and mercy. May the Spirit guide you in wisdom and grace, that by your service and ministry justice and mercy may be seen in all the earth.”

Another crown presented by the Archbishop of Canterbury. The Queen is being crowned with Queen Mary’s Crown. It has undergone a few minor changes and additions. Now it includes the Cullinan III, IV and V diamonds which were part of Queen Elizabeth II’s personal jewellery collection.
“May thy servant Camilla, who wears this crown, be filled by thine abundant grace and with all princely virtues; reign in her heart, O King of love, that, being certain of thy protection, she may be crowned with thy gracious favour; through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.”
Presented by the Keeper of the Jewel House to the Queen, this one has the same symbolism as the Sovereign’s Ring. For those who missed it, that is similar to a marriage ring: a symbol of promise and commitment, an unbroken bond both to the King and the country.
“Receive this Ring, a symbol of royal dignity, and a sign of the covenant sworn this day.”
And now we are going to watch a lot of what we just saw happen again as the Queen Consort’s Coronation gets underway. It is largely similar but this part of the ceremony charges the Queen with honouring and helping their spouse.
Interestingly, this is the first time this part of the ceremony has been conducted since 1937, with the Queen Elizabeth, later known as The Queen Mother. This is because the ceremony is only conferred on female consorts, so Prince Philip had no such ceremony.
The major difference is that the anointing of the Queen happens without a screen or canopy.

This is the part of the ceremony which has already stirred some controversy. In previous Coronations, at this point the Royal Dukes and hereditary peers would offer oaths of loyalty in order of the prestige associated with their title.
This time, in order to make the service feel more relevant and equitable to the common person, anyone who chooses to can swear an oath of allegiance. Many have blasted the inclusion of this homage as being ‘out of touch’, though no doubt royalists will be keen to say the words:
“I swear that I will pay true allegiance to Your Majesty, and to your heirs and successors according to law. So help me God.”
After this, another fanfare the Archbishop of Canterbury leads the people in cries of ‘God save The King’, to which the public respond ‘God save King Charles, Long live King Charles, May the King live for ever.”
Symbolically kneeling before the King, the Prince Of Wales offers his own oath and gives homage to become the ‘liege man’ of the Sovereign who has a mutual obligation to the Monarch.
“I, William, Prince of Wales, pledge my loyalty to you and faith and truth I will bear unto you, as your liege man of life and limb. So help me God.”
At this point, the Archbishop of Canterbury, on behalf of the Church of England swears his allegiance and fealty to King Charles and his heirs. Historically this part of the service was intended to head off future rebellions and ensure the loyalty of any powers which might challenge the King.
“I, Justin, Archbishop of Canterbury, will be faithful and true, and faith and truth will bear unto you, our Sovereign Lord, Defender of the Faith, and unto your heirs and successors according to law. So help me God.”
This will be the third time Justin Welby has sworn to honour the crown. Clergy have to swear an oath of allegiance to the monarch when they are ordained, then again when they are consecrated as a Bishop. This is because the monarch is the Supreme Governor of the Church of England.
A major moment in the Coronation comes next where the Archbishop of Canterbury sets the King in his crown on the throne. It is the culmination of all the proceedings and establishes the King’s reign.
Another quick anthem, this time written by Thomas Weekles. 2023 marks the 400th anniversary of his death.
Meant to summarise everything that has just happened, the blessing asks for God’s love, protection, grace and wisdom to be bestowed on the King for the rest of his reign.
For the first time, the Blessing is shared by Christian leaders from across the country. In order, they are: the Archbishop of York, the Greek Orthodox Archbishop of Thyateira and Great Britain, the Moderator of the Free Churches, the Secretary General of Churches Together in England, the Cardinal Archbishop of Westminster and finally the Archbishop of Canterbury.
The crowning is complete -- it's King Charles III.
The King is being crowned with the St Edward’s Crown, the rarest and most sacred of all the royal crowns.
Created in 1661 for the coronation of Charles II, it is one of the oldest symbols of the British monarchy.
It is a replacement of an earlier mediaeval crown that was melted down by parliamentarians in 1649 after the execution of King Charles I, during the English Civil War.
The original crown was thought to date back to the 11th century royal saint, Edward the Confessor, who was the last Anglo-Saxon king of England.
After 1685, the crown did not feature at a coronation for over 200 years. However, George V revived the tradition for his own coronation in 1911, and the crown has been used by every monarch since.
Read the full history of the crown here.
The moment all of this has been leading up to: the crowning. As with everything else, the King’s crown is a symbol. While we may look at it as another part of being King, its weight is meant to serve as a constant reminder to King Charles of all the promises and oaths he has made to his people, the church, and God.
The prayer of blessing spoken by the Archbishop of Canterbury now is the same one spoken at the Coronation of Queen Elizabeth II in 1953. The first cries of ‘God save The King’ at this point were first made in 1689 and have been a part of the Coronation service ever since.
Now the Archbishop of Wales and Primus of Scotland step forward with the Sceptre and Rod. Those both of them look like sceptres, the one with the cross is ‘The Sovereign’s Sceptre’ and represents temporal power and is associated with the virtues of good and wise governance. The one with the dove is known as the ‘the Rod of Equity and Mercy’ and represents the spiritual role of the King and his pastoral care of the people.
Next up we’ve got the Glove. This one is presented by Lord Singh of Wimbledon. This time the symbolism is all about the King being an advocate and challenger for the protection of his people’s honour. The second meaning is that it’s a remind of holding power gently, in a gloved had.
Similar to a wedding ring, The Sovereign’s Ring, presented now by Lord Patel, KT, is a symbol of a promise or commitment, an unbroken bond without end.
Another much-discussed element of the Coronation. The King is presented with the Orb by the Anglican Archbishop of Armagh who places it in his right hand while the Archbishop of Canterbury says some words, before the Archbishop of Armagh takes it back.
The Orb symbolises the Sovereign’s power over the world under the cross. This particular items dates back to the 17th Century and divided into three sections, one for each of the continents which the people of that time thought existed.
The Bishop of Durham now puts the Stole Royal, a sort of cape, around the King. Then Baroness Merron, the Prince Of Wales, and various assisting Bishops cloth him in the Robe. These clothes represent what the King has been given by God.
This is a new stole commissioned specifically for the Coronation as a gift by the Worshipful Company of Girdlers. It features Christian iconography, including the gridirons of St Lawrence and palm branches. The latter are a symbol of martyrdom.
Otherwise known as the ‘Bracelets of Sincerity and Wisdom’, these are given to Lord Kamall by the Dean who hands them to the King. The regalia being presented by peers from non-Christian faiths such as these represent the idea that there’s a mutual interdependence between faiths that the King is being invested by all people, not just the Christian Church.
Here the Lord President of the Council, Penny Mordaunt, exchanges the Sword of State for the Jewelled Sword of Offering who then passes it to the Archbishop. He offers a prayer then returns it to Mordaunt who carries it to the King and places it in his right hand. This is the first time the sword will be carried and presented by a woman. The Archbishop charges the King with using the sword for justice and peace and it is clipped to his girdle.
The sword is supposed to be seen as a metaphor for defence, advocacy, and justice, rather than as a violent weapon. It also references the word of God which St Paul likened to a sharp sword.
After some more words from the Archbishop of Canterbury on the theme of swords and justice, the King stands again. The sword is unclipped from the girdle and the King offers it to the Dean who places it on the altar. Penny Mordaunt takes the sword back now, she’ll carry it before the King from this moment onwards during the ceremony.
The Greek choir performing the psalm was chosen by King Charles to reflect his father, the late Duke of Edinburgh who was born a Prince of Greece, to remind the King of his father’s influence and service to the late Queen.
The first bit of the regalia to be presented to King Charles are the spurs. These particular ones were made for King Charles II and symbolise the time when the Monarch would have led the army. The words focus on courage and advocacy for those in need.
“Receive these spurs, symbols of honour and courage. May you be a brave advocate for those in need.”
Sky News presenter Kay Burley has claimed that Freddy Parker-Bowles, the Queen's grandson, is wearing his football kit beneath his pageboy outfit.
She said of the pageboys on Sky News: "One of them I believe is Freddy, her grandson - apparently he is a huge Tottenham Hotspurs fan and we're being told by his father, Tom, that he has his Tottenham Hotspurs strip on underneath his pageboy outfit - how very modern."
At the heart of the King’s Coronation is the ancient and invaluable jewel-encrusted regalia from swords to crowns - much of which have been used for more than 1,000 years.
But mystery surrounds the purpose of some of the objects, with royal experts admitting that despite their repeated use and historical significance, they have no idea what they were used for.
Most of the regalia was created during the reign of Charles II as replicas of medieval objects that were destroyed in the mid-17th century on the orders of Oliver Cromwell.
Among them is St Edward’s Staff, which was remade even though “no one was quite sure what it was for”.

The King is now dressed in the Colobium Sindonis, Supertunica and girdle. The first is a sleeveless linen tunic designed after the garments worn in the ancient world by many. Similar to the white robes worn by the clergy it is meant to symbolise purity and simplicity.
Next is the Supertunica, an embroidered golden coat which is a form of priestly robe, reminding everyone that The King has been consecrated before God and in the service of God.
The British monarchy has endured abdications, insurrections and myriad wars. But the only surviving relic from the tumultuous medieval period is an unlikely candidate.
A small silver gilt spoon is the only known artefact preserved from St Edward’s Regalia and it is set to play a major part in the Coronation of King Charles.
The Coronation Spoon was first recorded in the Royal Collection more than 600 years ago, in 1349, and has been used in every crowning ceremony of a British monarch since James I in 1603.
Dating back to the 12th century, it is the oldest paraphernalia used in coronations.
Read the full history of the artefact here.
Though it takes place behind a screen, the anointing is arranged around the Coronation Chair, a special throne made by the order of King Edward I, designed to hold the much-discussed Stone Of Scone; the ancient rock on which the Kings of Scotland were inaugurated. Usually it is held in Scotland but was lent by the Scottish Government and people of Scotland (though some nationalists are unhappy about this.)
Behind the screen the Archbishop of Canterbury will anoint the King, saving the following:
“Be your hands anointed with holy oil. Be your breast anointed with holy oil. Be your head anointed with holy oil, as kings, priests, and prophets were anointed. And as Solomon was anointed king by Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet, so may you be anointed, blessed, and consecrated King over the peoples, whom the Lord your God has given you to rule and govern; in theName of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.”
A new batch of Coronation oil was made for the for the ceremony from olives harvested from groves on the Mount of Olives, the burial place of the King’s paternal grandmother, Princess Alice of Battenberg.
The olives were pressed just outside Bethlehem and the oil was consecrated in Jerusalem.
The Archbishop of Canterbury revealed that it was his idea to use oil from Jerusalem to reflect the King’s “personal family connection with the Holy Land and his great care for its peoples”.
The formula was based on the same ancient recipe used to create the oil used at the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II in 1953 and her many predecessors dating back to Charles I in 1626.
However, in a break with tradition, it does not include any of the controversial animal products traditionally used, such as civet oil and ambergris, popularly known as whale’s vomit.
It was perfumed with essential oils – sesame, rose, jasmine, cinnamon, neroli, benzoin and amber – as well as orange blossom.

The thrilling anthem we're now hearing is Zadok the Priest, was first heard in this very same building at the coronation of King George II and Queen Caroline on 11 October 1727, Ivan Hewett writes.
It's been sung at the coronation of every monarch since, and the words have been said before that at every coronation, going right back to 973 AD when King Edagr was crowned.
Unlike his late mother’s 1953 Coronation, the King is being  anointed out of sight, enclosed behind a three-sided screen.
The new partition pays tribute to the Commonwealth and the King’s lifelong passion for sustainability.
In 1953, a canopy of cloth-of-gold was held over Queen Elizabeth II’s head for the anointing to protect her privacy, but the entire congregation could witness the moment as she was not shielded at the sides.
Read more here.
Exactly what it sounds like, this is the part of the service where the Archbishop of Canterbury receives the Coronation Oil and offers his thanks.
The oil itself comes from Greece. Specifically two olive groves on the Mount Of Olives, at the Monastery of Mary Magdalene and the Monastery of the Ascension. The former is the burial place of King Charles’ paternal grandmother, Princess Alice of Greece. These olives were then pressed in Bethlehem and are perfumed with sesame, jasmine, cinnamon, neroli, benzoin, amber, and orange blossom.

Becoming part of the Coronation service in the 14th Century, this is the start of the process during which King Charles will be anointed with holy oils. It echoes the themes of the gospel which have already been highlighted during the service.
A new element this time is that the Veni Creator Spiritus (meaning ‘Come Creator Spirit’) is being sung in the four traditional languages of the United Kingdom: English, Welsh, Scots Gaelic and Irish Gaelic) to celebrate the heritage of those communities and demonstrate the importance of keeping the languages alive.
There is a lot of regalia on display during the ceremony, so here's a quick look at what it all means.
We are here to crown a King, and we crown a King to serve.
What is given today is for the gain of all. For Jesus Christ announced a Kingdom in which the poor and oppressed are freed from chains of injustice. The blind see. The bruised and broken-hearted are healed.
That Kingdom sets the aims of all righteous government, all authority. And the Kingdom also sets the means of all government and authority. Jesus doesn’t grasp power or hold onto status.
The King of Kings, Jesus Christ, was anointed not to be served, but to serve. He creates the unchangeable law that with the privilege of power comes the duty to serve.
Service is love in action. We see active love in our care for the most vulnerable, the way we nurture and encourage the young, in the conservation of the natural world. We have seen those priorities in the life of duty lived by our King.
Today we have the honour of being in this Abbey with so many who show such love; you work with charities and organisations, you build community, you serve the nation in Armed Forces, in emergency services, and so many other ways. Next door are 400 extraordinary young people in St Margaret’s, whose lives speak of service. Around the world in the Realms and Commonwealth are so many more. You live your lives for the sake of others.
The unity you show, the example you give, is what binds us together and offers societies that are strong, joyful, happy and glorious. They bear heavy weights for us.
The weight of the task given you today, Your Majesties, is only bearable by the Spirit of God, who gives us the strength to give our lives to others. With the anointing of the Holy Spirit, the King is given freely what no ruler can ever attain through will, or politics, or war, or tyranny: the Holy Spirit draws us to love in action.
This is promised by Jesus who put aside all privilege, because, as the first reading tells us, God will give all things for our sake, even His life.
His throne was a Cross. His crown was made of thorns. His regalia were the wounds that pierced his body.
Each of us is called by God to serve. Whatever that looks like in our own lives, each of us can choose God’s way today.
We can say to the King of Kings, God Himself, as does the King here today, ‘give grace that in thy service I may find perfect freedom’.
In that prayer there is promise beyond measure, joy beyond dreams, hope that endures. By that prayer, for every King, every ruler, and, yes, for all of us, we are opened to the transforming love of God.

The King, who is known to carry his own fountain pen for when he is frequently called on to sign visitors' books during royal visits, grimaced when he screwed the top back on the pen after signing the Oath during the coronation service.
When he signed documents during his first Privy Council meeting in September, the King made many chuckle on social media when he gestured for an ornate pen holder to be taken away by an aide.
Dame Sarah Mullally, DBE, Dean of HM Chapels Royals steps up to deliver St Luke’s account of Jesus worshipping at a synagogue. Herein Jesus notes the hallmarks of how Christians understand the kingdom of God: healing, freedom, justice and peace.
A gospel acclamation which welcomes and celebrates the word of the gospel. The music was commissioned specifically for the Coronation by British composer Debbie Wiseman OBE. She was also the official composer and musical director of the Platinum Jubilee Celebration at Windsor in May 2022.
The first appearance of the Prime Minister at the ceremony. Here Rishi Sunak will be reading Colossians 1: 9-17, a selection chosen by the Archbishop Of Canterbury. Originally this was a letter written by St Paul to a Christian community in Colossae (now a part of Turkey) which held one of the first churches to be established after the resurrection of Christ.
The theme of the epistle is essentially a wish for the listener (in this case, the King) to have patience and strength in his new position.
A Collect is a summary and thematic type of prayer used at every Church Of England service, though this one has been written specifically for the Coronation. It continues to focus on the theme of loving service which the modern monarchy relies upon.
“Lord, enthroned in heavenly splendour: look with favour upon thy servant Charles our King, and bestow upon him such gifts of wisdom and love that we and all thy people may live in peace and prosperity and in loving service one to another, to thine eternal glory; who with the Father and the Holy Spirit reigns supreme over all things, one God, now and for ever. Amen.”
The Princess of Wales and Princess Charlotte are wearing Jess Collett x Alexander McQueen headpiece, Melissa Twigg writes, made with silver bullion, crystal and silver threadwork in a three-dimensional leaf embroidery.
Speculation has been rife for days as to whether the Princess of Wales would break with tradition and wear flowers in her hair or opt for a tiara - the result is somewhere between the two.
It also shows that she has carefully selected her clothes to illustrate her loyalty to the King, who has wanted to bring his passion for nature to the fore and to dial back the monarchy’s historic taste for dazzling jewellery.
From the Bearer of the Golden Spurs to the carrier of the silver baton, King Charles is being supported by a number of key individuals during the Coronation.
A total of 13 individuals and organisations were chosen by the Coronation Claims Office to perform historic ceremonial roles during the ceremony.
Applicants were asked to provide evidence they were directly descendants of those who had performed similar roles at previous coronations.
However, many wrongly believed they had a hereditary right to attend, often based on some family fable, with around 10 per cent to 20 per cent of the applications being so poor they warranted no further investigation.

“Gloria in excelsis” - usually associated with Midnight Mass at Christmas, this is one of the most ancient songs of the church, supposedly based on the song of the angels at the birth of Jesus. This version was written by composer William Byrd around 1592-1593.
Now that King Charles has made his legal and constitutional promises to the nation and its realms, he must now offer this prayer and his vows to God. The prayer was specifically composed for His Majesty alone, aiming to reflect the theme of loving service, inspired by Biblical language.
God of compassion and mercy, whose Son was sent not to be served but to serve, give grace that I may find in thy service perfect freedom and in that freedom knowledge of thy truth.
Grant that I may be a blessing to all thy children, of every faith and conviction, that together we may discover the ways of gentleness and be led into the paths of peace. Through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.
A simple prayer written by Archbishop Thomas Cranmer to be in 1549 published in ‘The Common Prayer’, the foundational text of the Church Of England’s doctrine and worship.
“Prevent us, O Lord, in all our doings with thy most gracious favour, and further us with thy continual help; that in all our works begun, continued, and ended in thee, we may glorify thy holy Name, and finally by thy mercy obtain everlasting life; through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.”
A special edition of the Bible has been made for every coronation since the joint one for William III and Mary II in 1689, and is used when the monarch swears the oaths.
The new edition of the King James Version of the Bible, made for King Charles, is bound in red leather and decorated in gold leaf, with the royal coat of arms surrounded by a ring of crowns and leaves, to represent the King’s love of the natural world.
Elizabeth II’s coronation bible was also bound in red leather but decorated with multiple EIIRs – her insignia. As she was presented with it, she was told: Here is Wisdom; this is the royal law; these are the lively oracles of God.

In this important part of the service, the King makes an oath that he will defend the church, peace, and the laws and customs of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. A new line was inserted before the traditional oath.
“Will you solemnly promise and swear to govern the Peoples of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, your other Realms and the Territories to any of them belonging or pertaining, according to their respective laws and customs?”
This reflects the late Queen’s wishes that the Anglican church should have a duty to protect the free practice of all faiths in the country.
Here the church is making it’s first ‘gift’ to the King in the form of ‘the Word Of God’. By accepting it, the King recognises that the word of God stands above all human laws.
“To keep you ever mindful of the law and the Gospel of God, as the Rule for the whole life and government of Christian Princes, receive this Book, the most valuable thing that this world affords. Here is Wisdom; This is the royal Law; These are the lively Oracles of God.”
Use of the word ‘lively’ is a suggestion that King should read the Bible so that it may speak to the way he governs.
The Recognition is the first element of the traditional English Coronation Rite, versions of which date back to King Edgar who was crowned in 973AD. The rite sees the King turn to each of the four sides of the ‘theatre’ to be presented to the people. Here the assembled crowds will shout ‘God Save King Charles’, affirming and acknowledging that the King is the one they recognise as Head of State.
The people making the declarations are the Archbishop Of Canterbury followed by Lady Angiolini, LT (A Lady of the Thistle representing the oldest Order Of Chivalry in Scotland), Christopher Finney, GC (Chair of the Victoria Cross & George Cross Association, chosen for distinguished service in the military), and finally Baronness Amos, LG (A Lady of The Garter, representing the oldest Order of Chivalry in England.)
The choir is singing Kyrie Eleison, a new commission for the Coronation which is being sung in Welsh for the first time.
The choir is joined by Sir Bryn Terfel, the Welsh bass-baritone singer.
The Archbishop of Canterbury is delivering the greeting from the High Altar, welcoming the congregation to the service.
The service starts with a blessing of God’s love, to which the congregation reciprocate the blessing: And with thy spirit.
The introductions lays out what is to take place and invites everyone to participate and share in the commitment to love and serve one another.
Their Majesties are taking part in a moment of silent prayer at the Chair of Estate ahead of the ceremony.
It is designed to allow the King to reflect, contemplate and bring themselves and the Coronation service before God.
As in 1953, it reflects Their Majesties’ homage to God before any person pays homage to them.
Samuel Strachan, the longest-serving chorister of the Chapel Royal, St James’s Palace, is greeting the King inside Westminster Abbey.
The 14-year-old, who attends the City of London School, will tell the monarch: "Your Majesty, as children of the kingdom of God we welcome you in the name of the King of Kings."
The King will reply before the service begins with the Recognition.

Two fragments from the True Cross - said to have been used in the crucifixion of Jesus Christ - have been incorporated into a new processional cross.
The fragments were gifted to the King by the Pope in March, and formally presented to the Royal Household by Vatican representatives at the Chapel Royal at St James’s Palace.
In what was hailed as a “significant ecumenical gesture”, the King requested that the shards be incorporated into a new cross that he commissioned for the Church in Wales to celebrate its centenary before becoming monarch.
Both fragments are shaped as crosses, one measuring 1cm and the other 5mm. They have now been set into the larger silver cross behind a rose crystal gemstone.
On the day of his Coronation, the cross will be used to lead the procession into Westminster Abbey, a decision said to reflect the King’s “deep and long standing affection for Wales”.

His Majesty King Charles wears a spectacular outfit, steeped in historical and military references, Bethan Holt writes.

King Charles and the Queen are making their way down the Mall in the Diamond Jubilee State Coach with huge pomp and pageantry surrounding them.
The Diamond Jubilee State Coach also celebrates hundreds of years of British history. Pieces of Henry VIII's warship the Mary Rose, Sir Issac Newton's apple tree and the stone of destiny are some of the many artefacts incorporated into the bodywork of the carriage.
The handrails are made from the Royal Yacht Britannia, while a wooden crown covered in gold leaf - which forms the centrepiece of the roof's decorations - was carved from oak from Nelson's flagship HMS Victory.
It also boasts fragments of 10 Downing Street, the royal box at Ascot, Sir Ernest Shackleton's Antarctic base, Hut Six at codebreaking centre Bletchley Park and one of Sir Edmund Hillary's Everest ladders, as well as timber from 30 palaces, castles and cathedrals, much of which was fashioned into small varnished squares and used to decorate the interior walls and door panels.
There is even a fragment of Florence Nightingale’s dress.

The King and Queen are travelling to Westminster Abbey in the Diamond Jubilee State Coach,  the most recent addition to the Royal Mews.
Built in Australia and first used in 2014, the three ton, 18ft-long coach boasts hydraulic suspension, a heating system, lighting, electric windows and air conditioning.
The carriage was originally intended to mark the late Queen’s 80th birthday in 2006, but took so long to be built that it was named instead in honour of the 60th anniversary of her accession in 2012.
By opting for the Australian-built coach, the King will neatly incorporate a Commonwealth element into the event.

In Westminster Abbey, where guests have taken their seats as early as 7am, the congregation heard a new piece Sacred Fire by classical and film composer Sarah Class, Ivan Hewett writes.
She was commissioned by The former Prince of Wales in 2021 to compose the anthem for His Majesty’s Terra Carta environmental initiative. For the Coronation, Class’s ‘ which will be performed by acclaimed South African soprano Pretty Yende. It  conjures imagery from the Bible.
We also heard Crown Imperial, an orchestral march by William Walton, commissioned for the coronation of King George VI in Westminster Abbey in 1937.
It is in the Pomp and Circumstance tradition, with a brisk opening contrasting with a broad middle section, leading to a resounding conclusion. The work has been heard at subsequent state occasions in the Abbey: the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II in 1953 and the wedding of Prince William in 2011.
The music before the ceremony is provided partly by the newly-formed Coronation Orchestra and the Monteverdi Orchestra and the English Baroque Soloists.
There's a division of responsibilities between the two orchestras: the Coronation Orchestra plays six of the new newly written pieces, the English Baroque Soloists and Monteverdi Choir perform grand music from previous ages.

The order of service for the Coronation is, by tradition, the work of many hands – Church, state and monarch. There has been much talk of how the King, one who makes his views known, wants a more modern, more inclusive ceremony.
But since this is, ultimately, a religious service – the Coronation sits within an Anglican Communion service – the final responsibility for what happens lies with the Archbishop of Canterbury, on this occasion the Most Rev Justin Welby.
So the innovations that will be seen, when compared with the order of service at the Coronation of Queen Elizabeth II almost 70 years ago, tell us as much about the 105th Archbishop of Canterbury as they do about our King.
And Welby risks being accused of trying to be everything to everyone and ending up pleasing no one – a charge that has been levelled at him throughout his nearly 11 years at Lambeth Palace.

Speaking ahead of the Coronation service on BBC Radio 4’s Thought for the Day, the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Most Rev Justin Welby, spoke of the expectations and burdens placed on leaders as well as every human’s fear of “letting people down”, Gabriella Swerling writes.
The Archbishop added:
Leaders of any kind must carry the weight of expectations, and we all do, and there is no shortage of people to remind them of what those are.
This morning the King will bear that weight. In a service full of ancient ritual, he will swear his loyalty to us all and publicly promise to bring justice, mercy and good government.
[...] No human being can meet expectations – other people's or their own – without help, neither can the King. A community, a family, a nation that serves and works together can find common strength in a world of need but in my experience the final difference. In an honest and humble prayer for help then hope comes alive when we acknowledge we need one another and God we make space for something truly remarkable to happen.
We open up the possibility that together we may do something much stronger, much bigger and much more significant than we would ever do alone. So together this weekend, let's come together and recommit ourselves to work together for the future we all want to see.
For most of the people waiting along the route, it’ll be all eyes on the gold state coach. For Marcus and Kate Seaton there is a certain member of the Household Cavalry they are eager to catch a glimpse of, Eleanor Steafel writes.

The 60-year-old from Saffron Walden was awarded a BEM for her services to the community during the Covid pandemic and received her invitation in recognition of her work organising meals for the elderly and vulnerable.
“I feel so lucky to be here and so honoured. I’ve always been a royalist but to be honest I thought it was a spam email,” she said. “I think Charles will make a great king. He already is. The Queen was wonderful but he’s more in touch. He doesn’t feel quite so distant and he’s moving the Royal family closer to the younger generations.”
Rail bosses and military officers managing the arrival and departure of 5,000 armed forces personnel and members of the public at London's Waterloo station for the Coronation have heralded "a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity".
Troops arrived at the UK's busiest station on Saturday morning before marching off to take part in the procession, in the biggest movement of military personnel on Britain's railways since Sir Winston Churchill's funeral in 1965.
Members of the Royal Navy, Army, RAF and Commonwealth forces arrived on seven South Western Railway trains and two chartered West Coast Railways trains, before marching over Westminster Bridge to assemble ahead of the coronation.
Sergeant Richard Flattery, of the Royal Logistics Corps, is working alongside police and railway security teams to manage the flow at Waterloo.
"It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity in my career," he said. "We've got the military police with us as well on standby and they're lining the route as well to make sure nobody is encroaching on the parade."
A lovely anecdote from India Hicks, the King’s goddaughter, this morning, who recalled how Charles had regularly sent her individual pieces from a dinner set on her birthday.
“Brilliantly, every year as a child, and slightly mysteriously when you’re eight, you’d get a gravy dish or a teacup,” she said.
“Of course, now as an adult I have a complete set of fine china dining. Most of the presents you give to a godchild are a piece of plastic that is completely immaterial later.
“It just shows that the man then was thinking in the most forward, progressive way.”
Ms Hicks told the BBC that the King had been an “incredibly considerate” godfather from the moment he attended her christening through to her confirmation.
“(He) never forgets birthday presents,” she added. “At my wedding, he sent me a lovely long letter… just someone who takes the times and really thinks about what he’s giving.
“I’ve had the most remarkable gifts all my life from him. Once, a beautiful bracelet with an I and an H entwined that he had designed, a clock for my christening with the date engraved into it…”
