https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.title: Me-me-me Britain’s only growth areas are entitlement and laziness
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.subtitle: The woman who sprayed activists with a hose at Chelsea is a heroine to an increasingly fed up silent majority
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.text:
Britain has found a new heroine in the lady who set a hose on the Just Stop Oil protesters who vandalised a garden at the Chelsea Flower Show. When several ecomaniacs started throwing orange powder paint across the plants of a display showcasing sustainability on Thursday, one middle-aged woman grabbed a hose and ever so casually soaked the intruders until she was stopped by a security guard.
As this most irritating of scenes unfolded at one of the most civilised events on Earth, I’m sure you were thinking the same as me: if only she had been within arm’s reach of a water cannon. Yet her remarkably restrained response to the selfish outrages committed by radical activists sums up the dignity of ordinary, decent people in the face of this offensive bunch of over-privileged rabble rousers.
The well-deserved drenching was emblematic of a Britain that has had it up to here with the sublime entitlement of campaigners who think they can spoil someone else’s hard work – and a day out to Chelsea – because they have something to shout about climate change.
We later learnt that the garden spoilers included Naomi Goddard, 58, a reported “flood expert” from Hebden Bridge, who warns of disaster in her quiet corner of West Yorkshire while apparently struggling to acknowledge the area has been prone to flooding for centuries.
She was joined by charity worker Stephanie Golder, 35, an activist from Southend, Essex, and support worker Rosa Hicks, 28, who doesn’t appear to see the hypocrisy in hectoring about the environment while having reportedly taken a year out to study in Australia. Privilege doesn’t even cover it. Don’t these women have jobs to go to?
While the Chelsea Flower Show was being shamelessly oranged, another trio of mimseys were kidnapping lambs from the King’s Sandringham estate, supposedly in the name of animal welfare.
Seemingly oblivious to the potential distress caused to the lambs by being separated from their flock, militants Rose Patterson, 33, Rosa Sharkey, 23, and Sarah Foy, 23, filmed themselves holding the animals in a van in a stunt anyone with any knowledge of farming knows will have left the bleaters terrified.
Despite apparently lacking understanding of livestock care, these morons actually think they are in a position to lecture others on animal welfare. Indeed, many “animal rights” activists appear blissfully unaware that being a herbivore does not make you an expert on anything, except perhaps vitamin B-12 deficiency. Yet on they go, ramming their marginal and extremist views down everyone else’s throats.
Sadly, entitlement seems to be becoming something of a running theme in this country. This week, we learnt that borrowing has risen to the second highest level ever for April, driven in part by surging welfare payments. More than five million people are now on out-of-work benefits according to some estimates, despite there being hundreds of thousands of job vacancies.
We all thought the era of people being better off by not working had ended with the introduction of Universal Credit. And yet, in this strange post-pandemic period, some people who could work are simply choosing not to. While that may be their right in a free society, where does it leave the rest of us?
All those people shunning jobs are necessitating an immigration policy that sees hundreds of thousands of workers imported into the country to plug the shortages. As Thursday’s immigration figures from the Office for National Statistics confirmed, net migration stands at an unprecedented 606,000. This, in turn, is fuelling a mass housing shortage and sky high rents along with a scarcity of school places and doctors’ appointments. It will inevitably place enormous pressure on Britain’s infrastructure, but our culture has become so consumed by me-me-me that nobody wants to connect the dots.
Of course, successive governments are to blame for creating a high tax, low wage economy where younger generations can no longer afford to get on the housing ladder. And, as well as failing to build enough houses, our elected representatives have been remiss in neglecting to train more homegrown medics, preferring the cheaper solution of issuing health visas to foreigners instead.
Similarly, by allowing campuses to be flooded with overseas students, they might well be limiting the number of British university entrants in a bid to keep tuition fees down for those lucky enough to gain a place.
Still, it is not just the fault of the powers that be that, to ape the famous Saatchi & Saatchi slogan from the 1970s, Britain isn’t working. These days, people seem to need to be actively encouraged to go out to work when it used to be a given.
Once upon a time, Britons had a moral impulse to work because they didn’t want to become a burden on the state. The consensus was that you shouldn’t take something out if you hadn’t put anything in, yet that seems to have evaporated into a narcissistic presumptuousness that you can do as little as you want and expect others to pick up the tab. People increasingly seem to think they are entitled to an easy life – paid for by the rest of us.
While I appreciate there has been a troubling rise in mental health issues and anxiety, particularly among the young, I cannot help but think that some of this could be down to a lack of purpose in life. For it used to be thought that work was positive for helping to manage conditions like mild depression by giving sufferers a sense of belonging and accomplishment.
Work was also a calling, a chance to help yourself, your family and even strangers. And thankfully, some young people – the most ambitious of them – still understand this. Ask a graduate trainee or an apprentice if they would like to work hard in an office and they will probably say yes. But their voices are drowned out by a metropolitan elite that appears so hooked on the convenience of Zoom that it has forgotten it is supposed to be passing on knowledge to the next generation.
These lazy elites were given a leg up, but now it’s a case of pull the ladder up, and damn the rest. Why should they care that others don’t have the luxury of working from home, so long as they can get their recycling bins emptied on time, and their organic food boxes delivered straight to the door? Some will be cheering on the antics of a small minority of Greta Thunberg devotees, who seem intent on getting in the way of people with actual jobs.
Many of the ills in this country today, from its sinking economy to the troublemaking of radical protestors, can be associated with our wider social crisis. Frankly, it’s a miracle that the fury of the sensibles has so far been contained to a bit of hose-waving.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.title: Why is the UK so soft on eco-protesters?
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.subtitle: On the Coronation eve the threat of climate protests loom but, thanks to a toothless legal system, the police have little power to stop them
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.text:
How should we deal with climate protesters? It’s a question that was front and centre in the minds of many after a Just Stop Oil (JSO) activist had their foot run over by a car in north London. The driver decided that a band of protesters in high-vis orange jackets were not enough of a deterrent to prevent them from continuing their journey down the Holloway Road while the activists were outraged that one of their own should be subjected to injury while peacefully protesting.
The police are now appealing for information. Critics are saying the Met should have intervened sooner to stop the protest from escalating. Just Stop Oil plans to protest indefinitely, yet according to the Metropolitan police, blocking the road does not meet the legal threshold of causing “serious disruption” – a phrase which is becoming increasingly contentious and difficult to define.
The policing model in the UK is built on the principle of “policing by consent”, based on nine principles set out in 1829. But 194 years later, that is causing frustration and concerns that we are being too soft on environmental protesters, especially compared to how they are treated in Europe.
“In many but not all policing systems in Europe, but particularly in southern Europe, the police are essentially an arm of the military so they tend to take an enforcement-led approach to policing,” says Rick Muir, director of the The Police Foundation, the UK’s policing think tank. “Our tradition is to police by consent and that means that you use force as a last resort. Before that, our police try to secure compliance of the law by voluntary means.”
Sir Mark Rowley, the Met commissioner, spoke last year of his frustration that officers could not do more to stop roads being blocked while Stephen Watson, the chief constable of Greater Manchester Police, has said forces do have the power to tackle demonstrators and should do so “very, very quickly” adding that if activists targeted his area they should not expect a “warm blanket and a cup of tea”.
Suella Braverman, the Home Secretary, has admitted that the police are sometimes seen as supporting militant protesters, “dancing along with them” and she has called for more “common sense policing”.
The Government has been accused of expediting new powers for the police to prevent disruption during the Coronation, giving them the ability to stop and search if they think protesters are carrying padlocks, superglue and bike locks and intend to use them to cause disruption.
“Locking-on” to other people, buildings and objects will also carry a maximum sentence of six months and an unlimited fine and police will be able to use their discretion as to whether the seize such materials or detain individuals. A lower threshold at when the police can intervene during slow-walking protests is also in the pipeline – although this amendment is still to be approved by the Commons and the Lords so not able to make a difference for this weekend’s activities.
“I think it’s a vanity project,” says Stewart Frost, senior lecturer in policing practice at Middlesex University. “I think the effect will be quite small. Yes, it may close a few loopholes and I think you will see these new powers being used over the coronation weekend – but there is better legislation already in place that is more fit for purpose.”
“The police have not got an easy job,” says Adam Wagner, barrister and human rights advocate at London’s Doughty Street Chambers. “They’ve got to interpret these brand new laws that were obviously rushed through in time for the coronation. They now have a few days to think about how they’re going to use them, if they’re going to use them, and how they’re also going to protect the right to protest – which despite all these laws, we still have.”
Wagner believes that far from being too lenient, the police have in fact been given too much “wiggle room” and lists the various pieces of legislation that could be used to curtail any protests at the coronation. He mentions the Highways Act (“the offence obstruction of the highway”), injunctions on major roads (“at the moment, there’s one applying to the entire strategic road network”) and the newly minted Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act of 2022, where “serious disruption” can now be criminalised (“That’s a very open term, and it includes very noisy protests”).
Blocking national infrastructure, such as railway lines, is now an offence under the new Public Order Act 2023 and then “there are specific orders that can be obtained by the police that can prevent mass gatherings in areas”. There are also, he says, laws relating to displaying threatening or abusive material and using threatening and abusive language – all of which have to be decoded by an individual. “Officers on the ground are going to have to decide, ‘Is this protest getting so noisy that it’s seriously disruptive? Am I going to have to start arresting people?’”
It’s an unenviable position. So much personal discretion is involved  – something that doesn’t always burden the police on the continent dealing with similar guerilla tactics from climate change activists.
Muir explains that the way policing works now requires the police to use their powers proportionately once they’ve weighed up the situation in front of them, keeping in mind the various laws – and in the case of road blocks that includes the Highways Act that allows them to move people on coupled with the Supreme Court ruling in 2019 that said a certain amount of disruption during protests is to be allowed. (Despite leaving the EU, the UK has committed to being subject to the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR) and Article 11 protects the right to hold meetings and demonstrations with other people – any UK legislation has to find a way to sit with that.) It’s a difficult line to tread.
“When it comes to public order, the police get it in the neck whatever they do,” Muir explains. “They get criticised for going in too hard, they get criticised for being too soft. And at the end of the day, in any free society, there is a balance between liberty and security and the police are right in the middle of that. They have to make these calls.”
So while decisive action by the police in France, Spain and Italy may look attractive from a distance, Muir believes that there’s a case of being careful what you wish for. “Back in the 19th century, Robert Peel’s whole idea with policing was that we don't want the police to be a repressive arm of the state, we want police to be ordinary members of the public who put on a uniform and get powers given to them when they’re doing that, and who are accepted by the community. So far, that has served us pretty well. I think people in this country would be very uncomfortable with military policing.”
Be as that may, exactly what are other countries doing that appears so much more decisive?
In April, German police resorted to drilling out a chunk of the tarmac around one protester’s hand, using a drill and a crowbar to free it from where it had been superglued to the road.
There’s no precedent for this here as the police must demonstrate that “their use of powers are necessary and proportionate” and doesn’t interfere with an individual’s right to protest. However, the British police do use ‘debonding liquid’ to dissolve glue and remove protesters before searching and arresting them. Over here, they can be removed and are, but they don’t just rip them off. They now have the power to arrest them for locking-on under the new Public Order Act 2023.
Germany already has tough rules when it comes to climate protests, as activists can be placed in preventative detention if they are suspected of participating in a disruptive demonstration. Police in the state of Bavaria started using a pre-emptive law amended in 2021 to extend the preventative detention period from 48 hours to 30 days.
The head of Germany’s national police union, Rainer Wendt, has called for Berlin to adopt the same tactic. In January, Greta Thunberg was photographed being hauled away and detained during a protest at a German village that was being demolished to make way for a coal mine. Punishment for such actions depends on what other laws are being broken and how much damage has been caused.
In France last November, a group of activists from the Dernière Rénovation group blocked Paris’s ring road in the western 16th arrondissement during rush hour, but they were removed within half an hour. (It took police in the UK 60 minutes to remove Just Stop Oil protesters from the M25 in November 2022, but by then tailbacks were at five miles.) Earlier in the year, Stage 10 of the Tour de France was obstructed by the same group. The demonstration only lasted 15 minutes as the activists were dragged away and arrested by police. But it’s not just the Gendarmes that can affect quick and decisive action. In July 2022, eight protesters from the same climate activist group were dragged off a Tour de France route by outraged fans before the police even had time to turn up.
They could have faced a two year prison sentence but in the end were just fined.
Over here, the Government’s Public Order Bill introduced a six month maximum jail term for people glueing or locking themselves to others, objects or buildings to cause disruption. Disrupting major transport works such as HS2 will carry a six-month sentence.
Austria has been shown to take a similarly hard line. In March, police detained 143 people from climate groups including Fridays for Future, founded by Thunberg, during a demonstration to protest the European Gas Conference in Vienna. They were criticised by Amnesty International for using heavy-handed tactics including pepper spray and batons.
“I’ve never seen that in the UK,” says Frost. “I don’t think it would be effective in the long term. It wouldn’t be a deterrent. And it would really undermine the Human Rights Act, the right to protest.”
Fifteen members of Rebelión Científica in Spain (the scientific arm of Extinction Rebellion) were arrested after throwing fake (and fully biodegradable) blood at Spain’s parliamentary building this week and, if convicted, they could be charged with criminal damage and public disorder, offences that lead to a maximum jail term of six years.
Rebelión Científica responded by saying that charging their members with such serious crimes for liquid that can be washed off by water is an “unprecedented and unjustifiable criminalisation of science”. Previously, in November, four people were detained in Madrid after activists glued their hands to the frames of two paintings by Francisco de Goya at Madrid’s Prado Museum. Last year in the UK, Just Stop Oil protesters glued themselves to Constable’s The Hay Wain in the National Gallery. They were freed on bail pending further police enquiries.
Other countries have utilised “fast-track” trials to prosecute climate activists more quickly. In Belgium, two members of Just Stop Oil Belgium (not associated with the British JSO) were fast-tracked to trial and sentenced to two months in prison for glueing themselves to Johannes Vermeer’s Girl with a Pearl Earring painting and the gallery wall.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/royal-family.title: Animal rights protesters steal the King’s sheep
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/royal-family.subtitle: Monarch’s passion for nature fails to save him from activists bent on disruption to advance their cause
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/royal-family.text:
The King has long been respected for his environmentalism and passion for sustainable farming.
But it seems that is not enough to prevent him becoming the latest target for animal rights activists who have struck at a farm on his Sandringham Estate.
Three women from the militant campaign group Animal Rising allegedly entered Appleton Farm, in West Newton, Norfolk, on Wednesday evening and stole three lambs, which they claimed were being prepared for slaughter.
After “liberating” the three lambs from their mothers, they took the animals – hastily named Sooty, Sunny and Sammy – to a “place of safety”, where they said they would live out the rest of their lives in peace.
To garner maximum publicity for their stunt, the three environmental activists then travelled 145 miles by car from Sandringham to Windsor Castle, where they tried to hand themselves into police.
Sarah Foy, 23, Rosa Sharkey, 23 and Rose Patterson, 33 - all experienced hands in direct action and disruptive protests - posed for pictures carrying placards with the slogan “I Rescued The King’s Sheep.”
But they were initially frustrated when officers at the royal residence refused to arrest them, saying they would need to speak to their colleagues at Norfolk Constabulary as it was not a Thames Valley Police matter.
Eventually though, they got their wish and were admitted to a police station in Slough, where they were arrested on suspicion of theft.
A spokesman for Thames Valley Police said: “Norfolk police are investigating reports three lambs were stolen from a farm in West Newton, Norfolk.
“Three women aged in their 20s and 30s voluntarily attended a police station in Slough and were arrested on suspicion of theft. They remain in custody.”
Ms Patterson, who is listed as a director of the campaign group, was previously arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to cause public nuisance following protests at the Grand National.
In an attempt to explain her actions ahead of her arrest, Ms Foy said: “Like anyone, animals want to live out their lives safely and without being used or exploited.
“Sadly that is not the case here at Sandringham, or anywhere they are used in our food system.
“That is exactly why we rescued three sheep today – three beautiful lambs who’ll now live their lives to the fullest. We urgently need a national conversation about our relationship with other animals and nature.
“The Royal family could be leading the way in this – they own land around twice the size of Greater London.
“It would be an incredible statement for them to fully commit to the transition to a safe, secure, plant-based food system and a rewilding programme. Mending our connection to animals is vital in tackling the climate and nature crises.”
A statement posted on the group’s social media account read: “Because of the bravery and compassion of these women, three babies Sammy, Sunny and Sooty will now be allowed to live their lives freely, in a safe space where they are not seen as objects or products, but as the sentient, emotional, lovely little individuals they are.
“By rescuing these lambs, Rose, Sarah and Rosa are hoping to not only give these gorgeous lambs a chance at a real life, but also to provoke conversation: we love animals, so why would we ever want to hurt them in this way?”
There are thousands of sheep on the 6,400 acres of the King’s Sandringham Estate. They are all fed on a forage-only diet and taken care of by shepherds highly experienced in animal husbandry.
The estate also prides itself on upholding the highest standards of animal welfare.
In 2018, an outdoor lambing sheep flock was introduced to contribute to the farm’s aims of improving soil structure and fertility.
They feed on a mixture of grass, clover, plantain and chicory for a diet rich in “protein and mineral sources”.
While grazing in the fields, the estate’s livestock can also shade under a variety of trees, including cider apple, plum, perry pear, quince, mulberry and walnut.
The King has introduced thousands of new sheep to the estate since taking over the running of the farm from the late Duke of Edinburgh in 2017.
The alleged raid at Appleton Farm is the latest in a string of stunts by the group, which is promising to step up its direct action campaign over the summer.
Last month, protesters disrupted the Grand National at Aintree. They have also threatened to target the Epsom Derby on June 2.
Up to 1,000 activists are thought to be planning to descend on the world-famous flat race with claims they will lock and glue themselves to perimeter fencing.
Having targeted the racing industry, the group, which is an offshoot of Extinction Rebellion, has now declared war on the farming and meat industry.
The incident at Sandringham is said to mark the start of a series of planned  “open rescues” throughout the summer.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2.title: Zelensky arrives in Saudi Arabia for talks with Arab leaders
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2.text:
Thanks for following today's liveblog.
Please follow along tomorrow for all the latest updates on Ukraine.
Russia’s general prosecutor has designated Greenpeace an “undesirable” organisation in the Russian Federation, the supervisory authority has said.
The prosecutor’s office is cited by state news agency TASS as saying that Greenpeace International is considered to “pose a threat to the foundations of the constitutional order and security of the Russian Federation.”
They added that the organisation’s environmental activities in Russia “are actually accompanied by active promotion of a political position, attempts to interfere in the internal affairs of the state and aimed at undermining its economic foundations.”
Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Greenpeace activists “engaged in anti-Russian propaganda, called for further economic isolation of our country and harsher sanction measures,” they added.
The wreckage of Russian missiles shot down over Ukraine indicates that the weapons were produced this year, with the country able to produce 67 missiles per month despite international sanctions, the deputy chief of the Ukrainian Defence Intelligence has said.
Ukrainska Pravda reported that Vadym Skibitsky told RBC-Ukraine news agency that the wreckage of missiles shot down over Ukraine indicates that the weapons had been produced in the first quarter of 2023.
Mr Skibitsky said: "They [Russians] bring Kalibrs to occupied Crimea at least twice a month. Russia is currently able to produce monthly about 25 Kalibrs, 35 pieces of Kh-101s, two pieces of Kinzhals, and five pieces of 9M723 ballistic missiles for the Iskander-M.
"Therefore, they manage to import components for producing missile weapons despite international sanctions."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged Arab leaders at the Arab League of leaders in Jeddah to "help protect" the Ukrainian people, including the Muslim community in Crimea.
He also thanked Saudi Arabia for helping negotiate the return of prisoners, and spoke of the Arab students who have visited and studied in Ukraine.
Mr Zelensky said:
Ukrainians has never chosen the war. Our troops didn’t go to other lands. We do not engage in annexation and plunder of other nation’s resources. But we will never submit to any foreigners or colonisers. That’s why we fight.
I am sure you will understand our main emotion, the main call I want to leave in Jeddah, a noble call to all of you to help protect our people including [the] Ukrainian Muslim community.
The Crimea and Tatar should remain an integral part of the Muslim community of the world, but Crimea were the first to suffer from the Russian occupation. Most of all, those who have had to suffer the occupation are Muslims.
Unfortunately there are some among the world, and here among you who turn a blind eye to those cases and illegal annexations. I am here so everyone can take an honest look, no matter how hard the Russians try to influence, there must be independence.

President Zelensky has visited Saudi Arabia for the first time ever "to enhance bilateral relations and Ukraine's ties with the Arab world," he said on Twitter on Friday.
"Political prisoners in Crimea and temporarily occupied territories, the return of our people, Peace Formula, energy cooperation. [Saudi Arabia] plays a significant role and we are ready to take our cooperation to the next level," he added.
The Kremlin has said that the "last remnants" of arms control agreements between Russia and the US were disappearing, after a group of US Republican lawmakers introduced a bill on Thursday to scrap the New START treaty on nuclear arms.
Earlier this year, Russian President Vladimir Putin suspended Russia's participation in the treaty, which caps the number of strategic nuclear warheads that the United States and Russia can deploy.
"We can now only state with regret that there are no serious, substantive contacts on these issues between Moscow and Washington," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
"Let's just say that the last remnants of the international legal framework in this area are slipping away."
Volodymyr Zelensky is set to fly to Japan to meet Western leaders amid rumours the US is willing to lift its ban on European allies to export jets to Ukraine, Daniel Martin reports from Hiroshima.
The Ukrainian president was only due to address the G7 summit virtually - as he did last year - but it emerged on Friday he would attend in person.
It comes amid signs of a breakthrough for Ukraine, which has been pressing allies to provide it with jets to help it defeat Russia.
Read more from The Telegraph's deputy political editor here.
A Russian court has fined popular ex-mayor and prominent Kremlin critic Yevgeny Roizman for comments he made about the Ukraine conflict, a lenient sentence in a string of trials targeting opposition figures in the country.
Mr Roizman received a fine of 260,000 roubles (£2,600) from a court in Yekaterinburg, where he used to be mayor, over charges of discrediting the Russian military, according to Russian news agencies.
Mr Roizman was accused of discrediting the army in a video he uploaded to YouTube in July 2022 in which he criticised the Russian invasion.
Mr Roizman is quoted as saying after the ruling: “In my view, under these circumstances, this is an acquittal.” The charge, to which he pleaded not guilty, carried a maximum sentence of five years.
President Volodymyr Zelensky says he has arrived in Saudi Arabia where he is due to meet with the Crown Prince, Mohammad bin Salman, and address an Arab League summit, James Rothwell reports.
The goal of the meeting is to meet with Arab leaders who have not yet taken a side in the conflict and lobby them to help defend Ukraine, sources told Reuters news agency.
Saudi Arabia and other members of the Gulf Cooperation Council generally regard Russia's invasion of Ukraine as a European crisis that does not require their involvement.
Last year Saudi Arabia and other members of the OPEC+ energy group, including Russia, pushed up oil prices, a move that benefitted Vladimir Putin amid an energy crisis triggered by his invasion of Ukraine.
Egypt, a leading Arab League state, had reportedly considered arming Russia against Ukraine but its position is now unclear, according to five US intelligence documents leaked in April.
A “rare” Russian drone has been uncovered by a Ukrainian soldier in the eastern region of Luhansk, Ukraine’s ministry of internal affairs has said.
A video shared online reportedly shows a Ukrainian soldier finding an Eleron-3 drone. Eleron-3 drones are reportedly used by Russia for aerial reconnaissance and short-range surveillance.
Ukraine has not captured many of this type of drone from Moscow’s forces.
In the video, the soldier said: “I managed to capture this new Russian drone relatively unscathed.
“Therefore, I consider the hunt to be successful, and interesting data from this drone was transferred to the relevant authorities of the Defence Forces of Ukraine.”
The UK has announced a new wave of sanctions against Russia, targeting 86 individuals and businesses “connected to Russia’s capacity to fund and wage the war”.
In a statement released on Friday morning, the Government said that the 86 designations target those connected to “Russia’s energy, metals, defence, transport and financial sectors”.
Companies which are connected to Rosatom, Russia’s state-owned nuclear energy company, “which are producing advanced materials and technology, including lasers, have also been sanctioned,” the UK Government said.
Foreign Secretary James Cleverly said on Twitter: “Today we’re increasing economic pressure – cracking down on Russia’s theft of Ukrainian grain and the remaining revenue sources that support its military machine.”
The G7 has issued a statement ahead of the summit in Hiroshima:
We, the Leaders of the G7, reaffirmed our commitment to stand together against Russia’s illegal, unjustifiable, and unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine. We condemn, in the strongest terms, Russia’s manifest violation of the Charter of the UN and the impact of Russia’s war on the rest of the world.
15 months of Russia’s aggression has cost thousands of lives, inflicted immense suffering on the people of Ukraine, and imperiled access to food and energy for many of the world’s most vulnerable people. We express our full sympathy and condolences to the Ukrainian people for their loss and suffering.
We salute the Ukrainian people for their brave resistance. Our support for Ukraine will not waver. We will not tire in our commitment to mitigate the impact of Russia’s illegal actions on the rest of the world.
Russian Defence Minister Sergei Shoigu has inspected the headquarters of the Russian forces fighting in the Zaporizhzhia region in southern Ukraine, state news agency TASS is reporting, citing the ministry of defence.
Mr Shoigu listened to the report from the commander of the troops in the area “on the situation and the implementation of combat missions of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation  in the main tactical areas”, the outlet reported.
The G7 leaders have ensured that Ukraine has the budget support it needs for this year and the early part of 2024, as they renewed their commitment to provide both financial and military support to the country.
In a statement at the summit in Hiroshima, the leaders said: "Today we are taking new steps to ensure that Russia’s illegal aggression against the sovereign state of Ukraine fails and to support the Ukrainian people in their quest for a just peace rooted in respect for international law.”
Washington will not block the export of F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by European countries, allies have been told, despite President Joe Biden’s previous reluctance to send warplanes to the country.
The Biden administration has informed European allies that they will not face opposition from Washington should they wish to send F-16s to Ukraine, the Washington Post reported.
Significant progress had been made by Ukrainian officials in convincing The Netherlands to send F-16s earlier this year, but countries must get approval from Washington before exporting the US-made planes because of third-party transfer agreements made as part of purchasing the jets.
There had been reports that the Biden administration was at odds with Europe over whether to supply Ukraine with the jets, and that the US had refused to allow Western allies to train Ukrainian pilots on the aircraft, despite impassioned pleas from Kyiv.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is to attend an Arab League meeting in Saudi Arabia, a source has told Reuters.
Mr Zelensky is on his way to the meeting, from where he will then travel onto the G7 meeting in Hiroshima, Japan on a French government plane.
The US has overestimated the value of the kit it has sent to Ukraine by $3 billion (£2.4 billion), officials have admitted.
The calculation may open the way for more weapons being sent to Kyiv.
The error was the result of assigning a higher than warranted value on weaponry that was taken from US stocks and then shipped to Ukraine, two senior defence officials said on Thursday.
Read more on this story here.
Ukraine’s air defences have repelled another Russian air attack early on Friday morning, destroying 19 out of 28 drones and missiles launched, according to the Ukrainian military.
Air force spokesman Yuriy Ihnat told Ukrainian television: "Three calibre missiles launched from the Black Sea and 16 drones were shot down. Shelling continues on an almost daily basis."
He added that "not all targets were hit.”
In the central city of Kryvyi Rih, at least two people have been injured, one seriously, after Russian strikes in the region.
The Governor of the Dnipropetrovsk region, Serhiy Lysak, wrote on Telegram that a private industrial complex was struck, seriously injuring a 64-year-old woman.
A fire also broke out in a four-storey building, where a man sustained minor injuries.
The head of the Wagner Group mercenary force, which has spearheaded the fighting in Bakhmut for several months, has said that the city is unlikely to fall to his forces in the next two days.
According to Yevgeny Prigozhin, Ukrainian forces are holed up in a makeshift “fortress” in the south of the front line city, while fighting continues around them.
In a voice message uploaded to Telegram, Mr Prigozhin said: "Bakhmut has still not been taken. Bakhmut is unlikely to be taken either tomorrow or the day after tomorrow.”
"There is a quarter known as the 'Airplane' - it is like an impregnable fortress from a bed of multi-storey buildings in the southwest of Bakhmut, where incredibly heavy battles are going on."
Washington will not block the export of F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by European countries, allies have been told, despite President Joe Biden’s previous reluctance to send warplanes to the country.
Earlier this week, Rishi Sunak announced the creation of an international coalition of countries that would aim to provide F-16s, which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had requested from western allies.
Kyiv city council has renamed two metro stations, one station under construction and several streets with names with some connection to Russia, in response to the invasion.
The Friendship of Peoples metro station will from now on be called ‘Zverinetskaya’ (after the name of a historical district of Kyiv), and Leo Tolstoy Square station became the Square of Ukrainian Heroes.
At the beginning of the year, the authorities held a vote for the city’s residents on the renaming of the metro stations, with the majority voting for the names which were approved on Thursday by the city council, Radio Svoboda reported.
The Kyiv council also renamed 26 streets and other city objects on Thursday, the outlet reported.
The city’s mayor Vitaly Klitschko said that 314 objects in the city have been renamed in total. Mr Klitshchko wrote on Telegram: “The process of derussification in Kyiv continues.”
In its latest daily intelligence update, the UK ministry of defence has said that Thursday’s train derailment near the Crimean city of Simferopol “will disrupt deliveries of supplies and potentially also weaponry” to Russia’s Black Sea Fleet.
The defence ministry added: “Any sabotage in this sensitive area will further increase the Kremlin’s concerns about its ability to protect other key infrastructure in Crimea.”
The Russian-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said in a statement on Telegram on Thursday that a freight train carrying grain was derailed in the Simferopol district and that nobody was injured.
Ukrainian forces have continued to advance in the eastern city of Bakhmut, the country's deputy defence minister said.
Hanna Malyar wrote on Telegram on Thursday afternoon: "Today the enemy attacked Bakhmut all day. All attacks were repelled by out defenders.
"As of now, we control the south-western part of Bakhmut."
Ms Malyar added: "The enemy also attacks the outskirts north of Bakhmut. The attacks were repulsed. In some areas, our troops are advancing 500 metres."
The head of the Wagner Group, Yevgeny Prigozhin, had accused the Russian army on Thursday of retrating in Bakhmut, leaving his own fighters exposed.
Volodymyr Zelensky reportedly plans to travel to Japan to join Group of Seven (G7) leaders.
Reuters, citing an anonymous European Union source, reported the Ukrainian president will fly to Hiroshima on Sunday.
The United States and other G7 nations, meanwhile, are set to unveil new sanctions and export controls targeting Russia over its war against Ukraine.
Officials were still hashing out the details of their final announcements on Russia.
Russian forces have been enhancing defensive positions in and around the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant ahead of an expected counter-offensive in the region.
New trenches have been dug around the city and more mines have been laid around Europe’s biggest nuclear plant, located  in the south of Ukraine, four witnesses told Reuters.
Surveillance cameras at the plant point north across a wide reservoir and towards Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Russia had set up firing positions atop some of the plant’s buildings for some time, with nets erected as a possible deterrent to drones.
Good morning and welcome to today's Ukraine liveblog.
We will be guiding you through all the latest updates on Ukraine.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.title: Chris Packham Just Stop Oil film may harm BBC impartiality, campaigners say
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.subtitle: Springwatch presenter is working on a documentary for Channel 4 on climate change protests
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.text:
Chris Packham could cause “reputational damage” to BBC impartiality by filming a new documentary about Just Stop Oil and the disruption used by climate change protesters, campaigners have said.
The naturalist, who presents Springwatch for the broadcaster, was seen at a slow march carried out by the eco-group in central London near the Strand on Friday.
He was being filmed by Channel 4 documentary makers and explained that the new documentary would look at “how disruptive we have to be” in order to protest successfully.
Tim Bonner, chief executive of the Countryside Alliance, warned that the decision to make the documentary, and express his support for the protesters, risked causing a new impartiality row with the BBC.
He said: “Groups like Just Stop Oil and Animal Rising are simply alienating the public with their daft stunts and selfish behaviour.
“Chris Packham should be very careful aligning himself with groups that cause so much misery to hardworking people, not least because of the reputational damage to the RSPCA and the BBC whom he is closely associated with.”
He added: “A documentary about the actions of these groups, presented by a person who has expressed his clear support for them, is unlikely to ever be truly impartial.”
Andy Mayer, chief operating officer at the Institute of Economic Affairs, also questioned Mr Packham’s objectivity.
He said: “Some will question whether Packham is a neutral choice for a public broadcaster – after he only last month cheered on the criminal obstruction of Dartford bridge by Just Stop Oil as an ‘enormous act of bravery’.”
Mr Packham was appointed chairman of the RSPCA earlier this week and Mr Bonner said it was a “strange decision from an organisation which has done so much to build its reputation in recent years”.
At the Just Stop Oil protest on Friday morning, Mr Packham told PoliticsJoe: “I’m making a documentary for Channel 4 about the future of climate protesting.
“Is it working? If it isn’t working, what are we going to do?
“Because we need to find a solution basically, and is protest a part of that solution? Where should we go? How disruptive do we have to be? Are we looking at... generating... mass public protest, or do we have to go even further and direct violence at property, fossil fuel infrastructure?”
He also expressed concern over the controversial new public order bill and warned it set a dangerous precedent if people were simply arrested for “wearing a t-shirt”.
He previously triggered an impartiality row in 2013 after branding government officials “brutalist thugs, liars and frauds” in a series of tweets.
A Channel 4 spokesman confirmed they would be making a documentary.
They said: “Chris is filming a documentary about climate change. This includes observational filming at protests.”
The BBC declined to comment but it is understood Packham’s role as a freelance presenter means he is not subject to the same strict impartiality guidelines as BBC staffers.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.title: Millionaire Labour donor to match public donations to Just Stop Oil
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.subtitle: Entrepreneur Dale Vince says he is ‘proud to donate’ to the protesters amid calls for Sir Keir Starmer to distance himself from the group
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.text:
One of Labour’s biggest financial supporters has pledged to match any donations to Just Stop Oil in the next 48 hours.
Dale Vince, a green energy entrepreneur, said the public should donate to the “brave people who are currently slow marching, causing disruption and risking their freedom”, amid calls for Sir Keir Starmer to distance himself from the group.
Mr Vince has donated more than £1.5 million to Labour and said on Wednesday that he had spoken to Sir Keir, the party’s leader, “last week on the phone”.
The Conservatives have accused Labour of being “in bed” with Just Stop Oil and called for Sir Keir to return any donations from Mr Vince’s company.
In an email to Just Stop Oil supporters on Wednesday morning, the founder of the green energy firm Ecotricity said he would double any donations “pound for pound”.
“There is no better time to make a financial contribution,” he said.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Wednesday, a shadow cabinet minister said it was “perfectly legitimate” for Labour to accept donations from Mr Vince, despite his association with the protest group.
Nick Thomas-Symonds said his party has been “extremely clear on our views on Just Stop Oil” and that Mr Vince is perfectly entitled to “give money to other causes”.
“If he wishes to give money to other causes that’s up to him, but it can hardly be said that this affects our views as a Labour Party on Just Stop Oil,” he said.
In Mr Vince’s email to Just Stop Oil supporters, he said: “I was on the front page of Monday’s Daily Mail and Radio 4 this morning for supporting Just Stop Oil, like that’s a crime or something.
“Along with thousands of others, I am proud to donate vital funds to the cause.
“I’m inviting you to join me in supporting the brave people who are currently slow marching, causing disruption and risking their freedom to save us from the climate crisis.
“If you give a donation in the next 48 hours I will match it, pound for pound.
“Winning this argument is all that matters.
“The ordinary people powering Just Stop Oil need our support to keep on doing what they are doing so effectively - and ultimately bring about the change we all demand.”
His email said that a £10 donation will pay for a high-visibility jacket for a protester, £50 will buy a second-hand smartphone “to film a slow march” and £100 “can buy the banners needed to send our message loud and clear”.
Just Stop Oil has brought roads to a standstill across the UK in recent weeks with “slow marching” protests that police have often been powerless to prevent.
The group has also disrupted major events including football matches, the World Snooker Championship and the Chelsea Flower Show.
Labour has been accused of allowing the eco tycoon to dictate its policy on energy issues, after it pledged to halt all new oil and gas drilling licences if it wins the next election.
Suella Braverman, the Home Secretary, has said Labour is “in bed” with Just Stop Oil, while Greg Hands, the Tory chairman, has called for Sir Keir to return the money.
On Wednesday, Mr Hands wrote to Anneliese Dodds, the Labour chairman, to “raise further concerns about the Labour Party’s relationship with the extremist organisation Just Stop Oil” and accuse the party of an “ideological vendetta against British energy independence”.
He added: “If you do not return this protest money the public will naturally assume that Labour and Just Stop Oil’s goals are one and the same.”
Speaking to the same programme, Mr Vince defended his contributions and revealed he had spoken to the Labour leader twice on the phone.
“I think it is a desperate stretch for the Right-wing press and Tory MPs actually to be saying there’s a link here, that this money should be given back,” he said.
“The money is not dodgy. I’m not dodgy. It’s all tax paid. I am completely transparent.”
He insisted there is “no link” between the money he donated to Labour and its policy on oil and gas.
The Telegraph understands that Mr Vince and Sir Keir did not discuss the policy in their discussion last week.
It comes after The Telegraph revealed that Mr Vince received £309,000 in furlough money during the pandemic. In the same period, he donated £770,000 to Labour.
Treasury sources said he should repay the public money if he did not need it to keep his business afloat.
“The point of furlough was to help keep people in work, not allow companies to make donations to Labour,” one said.
“It is obvious Dale Vince’s company didn’t need the support, so he should voluntarily repay the money.”

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/rugby-union/.title: Players and fans turn on Just Stop Oil protesters as Premiership Rugby final interrupted
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/rugby-union/.subtitle: England flanker Tom Curry helps drag one invader off pitch at Twickenham, while crowd showers them with beer and other projectiles
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/rugby-union/.text:
Just Stop Oil protesters were showered with beer by rugby fans as they brought the Premiership final at Twickenham to a halt.
Two men leapt over a knee-high barrier to run onto the pitch and release a cloud of orange paint, 20 minutes into the game between Sale Sharks and Saracens.
Sale and England flanker Tom Curry helped remove a protester from the pitch, grabbing his jeans and helping stadium staff lift him away, while Sale captain Jono Ross had to be restrained from physically engaging the other man.
Ross, after the final match of his career, said: “I don’t agree with what they do. I don’t agree with it at all. It is completely against everything I believe in.
“Then to come into sporting events and ruin sporting events week in week out, I don’t agree with it. I don’t agree with what they stand for.”
Saracens and England second row Maro Itoje said: “You can't pay too much attention to it. Fair play to the guys who are tackling them. I was just conserving my energy.”
The demonstration drew boos from the crowd, who threw beer and other projectiles at the pair as they were escorted out by stewards.
They were subsequently arrested on suspicion of aggravated trespass and criminal damage.
It comes two days after a Just Stop Oil protest at the Chelsea Flower Show, where demonstrators were hosed down by an incensed onlooker.
Just Stop Oil, which is demanding a halt to any new licences for oil, gas and coal projects, has named the two men as Dr Patrick Hart, a 37-year-old Bristol GP, and construction worker Sam Johnson, 40, from Essex.
Dr Hart claimed he had invaded the rugby pitch because it was his “duty as a doctor”.
Dr Hart continued: “In the same way the tobacco companies lied to us that tobacco was safe, the scrum of fossil fuel companies and corrupt politicians have been lying to us.
“They are keeping us addicted to fossil fuels, even though they know it’s killing us. I am not prepared to let them get away with mass murder.”
Referee Luke Pearce stopped play for several minutes as the protesters were taken off the pitch. Saracens scored a penalty try once the match had restarted.
Alex Sanderson, Sale’s director of rugby, said: “[My] reaction was just ‘what’s the next job’. I can’t run on and throttle them myself. That did create a break in the game from which they scored off the back of. It just shows the intensity of concentration you need.”
The apparent ease with which the men made their way onto the pitch is likely to raise questions about the stadium's security arrangements.
Twickenham Stadium paid tribute to its stewarding team, saying they “acted quickly and decisively”.The demonstrators drew online condemnation, with one person – apparently present at the match – calling them “muppets” and urging them to “let the rugby play on”.
Since its campaign began last year, Just Stop Oil claims that more than 2,000 members have been arrested and 138 sent to prison.
At the Chelsea Flower Show on Thursday, three Just Stop Oil demonstrators crossed the barrier into an award-winning garden and threw its orange powder on the plants.
A woman responded by taking a nearby hose and dousing protesters in water.
Security staff for the Royal Horticultural Society eventually managed to shepherd the trio out of the showground, where they were arrested.
In April, the group disrupted a match at the World Snooker Championship, with a man tipping orange paint on a table at the Crucible in Sheffield.
The Met said in a statement: “Two men have been arrested after paint was thrown on the pitch during the rugby union final at Twickenham today.
“The men were both arrested on suspicion of aggravated trespass and criminal damage. They have been taken into custody.”

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.title: Watch: Workman handcuffed after shoving Just Stop Oil protesters on Blackfriars Bridge
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.subtitle: Video shows police officers intercepting man as he attempted to remove protesters from road
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/05.text:
A workman has been handcuffed by police on Blackfriars Bridge after a Just Stop Oil protester was shoved to the ground in front of officers.
Footage captured at the protest showed a man, dressed in bright orange work gear, apparently attempting to remove demonstrators from the carriageway as they slowly walked backwards over the bridge.
Video shows police officers intercepting the man as he attempted to remove a second protester from the middle of the road. The incident comes just days after a man was filmed confronting Just Stop Oil supporters near the Tower of London.
Motorists caught up in the protest appeared to show support for the man as they beeped their horns in frustration at the standstill.
One voice is heard saying "absolutely disgusting" as the man is handcuffed by two police officers. Reports on social media suggested the man had been arrested but police said none had been made.
Police said: "At around 08.25hrs, officers detained a male member of the public for common assault after an altercation between him and two Just Stop Oil protesters on Blackfriars Bridge this morning.
"There have been no arrests. Police are investigating the matter.
Police said they were called to Blackfriars Bridge just before 8.30am to reports of protesters walking slowly in the road.
An order was imposed 10 minutes after officers arrived on the scene and the group moved out of the road a few minutes after it was given.
Just Stop Oil later addressed the incident on its Twitter feed.
"This is an impossible situation.
"Do we disrupt other ordinary people, like this man, arrested for lashing out today, or just sit back and watch everything burn?
"That's where our government has left us. More and more people are realising taking action is the right thing to do."
It comes as Just Stop Oil demonstrators also targeted Tower Bridge and London Bridge on Tuesday morning.
The group tweeted: "45 people, in three groups, are marching on three major routes taking them over Blackfriars Bridge, London Bridge and Tower Bridge.
"They are demanding no new oil, gas or coal projects in the UK."
